## 6. Conclusions This work deals with the integrated scheduling problem of production and predictive maintenance in permutation flowshops. This problem is characterized by flexible maintenance activities scheduled based on PHM outputs. Metaheuristic approaches seem to be the best and most practical choice to solve such an NP-hard problem. Among a large number of swarm intelligence-inspired methods, artificial bee colony (ABC), simulating the foraging behaviour of honey bees, has been successfully applied to different variants of scheduling problems. Hence, in this study, we develop an ABC algorithm with an efficient search process, to minimize the total completion time (Makespan) of the schedule. The main idea is to design adapted search procedures with appropriate structures to balance the exploration and exploitation of the search. A statistical analysis was used to accurately calibrate the ABC parameters. Comprehensive experiments were carried out to assess the performance of the proposed ABC compared to a VNS algorithm from the literature, dealing with the same problem. Results analysis shows that the proposed ABC is more efficient, providing better solutions in terms of Makespan minimization, in a shorter computational time. Technologies 2024, 12, 45 While the proposed ABC algorithm has demonstrated good results, some improvements can be considered. One potential enhancement axis involves the integration of a more robust selection scheme of the neighborhood structures by the employed bees. Moreover, the hybridization of ABC with other local search methods allows them to leverage their comple mentary strengths. Considering the average earliness/tardiness of maintenance interventions, the proposed ABC seems to be less performant. Indeed, this criterion was not tackled in this paper. Hence, a promising perspective would be to develop a multi-objective ABC algorithm where both production and maintenance criteria are simultaneously optimized. # An effective heuristic for flexible job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities
Shijin Wang <sup>a,\*</sup>, Jianbo Yu <sup>b</sup>
<sup>a</sup> Department of Management Science and Engineering, School of Economics & Management, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China <sup>b</sup> College of Mechatronics Engineering and Automation, Shanghai University, Shanghai 200072, China

## a r t i c l e i n f o
Article history: Received 12 September 2009 Received in revised form 25 February 2010 Accepted 18 May 2010 Available online 24 May 2010
Keywords: Flexible job-shop scheduling problem Availability constraints Filtered beam search Preventive maintenance

## a b s t r a c t
Most production scheduling problems, including the standard flexible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP), assume that machines are continuously available. However, in most realistic situations, machines may become unavailable during certain periods due to preventive maintenance (PM). In this paper, a flexible job-shop scheduling problem with machine availability constraints is considered. Each machine is subject to preventive maintenance during the planning period and the starting times of maintenance activities are either flexible in a time window or fixed beforehand. Moreover, two cases of maintenance resource constraint are considered: sufficient maintenance resource available or only one maintenance resource available. To deal with this variant FJSP problem with maintenance activities, a filtered beam search (FBS) based heuristic algorithm is proposed. With a modified branching scheme, the machine availability constraint and maintenance resource constraint can be easily incorporated into the proposed algorithm. Simulation experiments are conducted on some representative problems. The results demonstrate that the proposed filtered beam search based heuristic algorithm is a viable and effective approach for the FJSP with maintenance activities.

## 1. Introduction
Due to their importance both in the fields of manufacturing industries and operations research, production scheduling and maintenance planning have been received considerable attention both in academia and in industry. However, in practice, production scheduling and maintenance planning are typically made independently despite the implicit common goal of maximizing equipment productivity between them (Cassady & Kutanoglu, 2003, 2005).
Production scheduling is to allocate a limited set of resources to a number of jobs with optimization of one or multiple system criteria over time, while taking various constraints into account. Most of them assume that machines are always available at constant speed. They either ignore equipment failure or treat it as a random event (Cassady & Kutanoglu, 2003). Although reactive scheduling (or rescheduling) considers response scheduling after machine breakdown, it does not consider the practical requirement of high reliability for some equipment (e.g., furnace in steel plant, thermal generating units in power system (Mohanta, Sadhu, & Chakrabarti, 2007)). Reactive scheduling does not radically improve the reliability of machines either. Moreover, too often rescheduling may make the production system into a kind of chaos, because rescheduling leads to rearrangement of supporting resources (e.g., personnel, spare parts, and material handling devices). Therefore, a more realistic scheduling model should consider the machine availability constraint. This helps reducing the frequency of rescheduling and improving the robustness. Maintenance activities, especially preventive maintenance (PM), can restore the reliability of machines before it goes to breakdown. However, on one hand, maintenance activities take time that could otherwise be used for production scheduling; on the other hand, industrial applications cannot ignore the forecasted maintenance operations on the machines (Mauguiere, Billaut, & Bouquard, 2005). Therefore, the problem of simultaneously scheduling production jobs and maintenance activities obtains great attentions in recent years.
Preventive maintenance planning is usually generated in a maintenance system, like Computerized Maintenance Management Systems (CMMS) and Asset Management System (AMS). Preventive maintenance planning requires some pre-scheduled or reserved unavailability interval of machines. Therefore, production scheduling with maintenance activities is also treated as availability constraint of machines in the literature. Schmidt (2000) has reviewed most results related to deterministic scheduling problems with availability constraints published before 1998. After Schmidt’s work, many efforts are devoted to the production scheduling with maintenance activities in different machine environments with different job characteristics and different optimality criteria.

In the single machine context, Graves and Lee (1999) considered the scheduling problem with semiresumable<sup>1</sup> jobs and two maintenance intervals of a fixed duration on a single machine to minimize either total weighted completion time or the maximum lateness. Cassady and Kutanoglu (2003) proposed an integrated model that simultaneously determines production scheduling and preventive maintenance for a single machine in terms of the total weighted tardiness of jobs. This model is further extended into a similar model in terms of total weighted completion time in Cassady and Kutanoglu (2005). Compared with the total enumeration procedure in Cassady and Kutanoglu (2005), Sortrakul, Nachtmann, and Cassady (2005) presented heuristics based on the genetic algorithm (GA) for the same model. The job characteristics considered in these three papers are resumable and non-preemptive for PM. Chen and Liao (2005) studied the deterministic and probabilistic models of a single machine problem with different maintenance situations and resumable jobs with respect to the minimization of number of tardy jobs. The research is employed into a textile company. Ji, He, and Cheng (2007) analyzed the worst-case ratio of the LPT (longest processing time) dispatching rule for a single machine scheduling problem with nonresumable jobs and several periodic maintenance in terms of makespan minimization. Chen (2008) presented two optimization models and a heuristic for a single machine scheduling problem with nonresumable jobs and with flexible and periodic maintenance to minimize the makespan. Chen (2009) proposed a heuristic based on Moore’s algorithm and a branch-and-bound (B&B) algorithm to a single machine problem with periodic maintenance and nonresumable jobs with respect to the minimization of number of tardy jobs.
In the parallel machine context, Lee and Chen (2000) extended the work of Graves and Lee (1999) to parallel machines with nonresumable jobs to minimize total weighted completion time. Gharbi and Haouari (2005) considered the identical parallel-machine scheduling problem with availability restrictions for both jobs (release time and delivery time constraints) and machines. The objective is to minimize the makespan and they presented an exact branch-and-bound algorithm to solve this problem. With the objective of makespan minimization, Liao, Shyur, and Lin (2005) studied the two-parallel machine problem with only one machine unavailable for a fixed and known period. Both nonresumable and resumable cases are considered and the problem is solved with modified methods based on the Two-Machine Optimization (TMO) algorithm. Then, Lin and Liao (2007) extended the same problem to the case where each machine has a fixed and known unavailable period. Lee and Yu (2008) discussed a parallel-machine scheduling problem with the objectives of minimization of the expected sum of weighted completion times and the expected number of tardiness jobs, respectively. Both resumable and nonresumable cases are studied. Liao and Sheen (2008) analyzed the parallel-machine scheduling problem with machine availability and eligibility constraints while minimizing the makespan. The problem is formulated into a maximum flow problem and a binary search algorithm is proposed. Mellouli, Sadfi, Chu, and Kacem (2009) considered the identical parallel-machine scheduling problem with availability constraints and total completion time criterion. Three exact approaches (mixed integer linear programming based methods, a dynamic programming method and a branch-and-bound method) are proposed as well as some heuristics adapted from the Shortest Processing Time (SPT) rule.
Because of their fundamental characteristic and simplicity, single machine and parallel-machine scheduling problems with availability constraints under different criteria have been extensively studied. Readers are referred to Ma, Chu, and Zuo (2010) for a relative comprehensive overview.
Recently, scheduling problems with availability constraints in more complicated environments, such as flow shop, job-shop and hybrid environments, have being attracted more and more attentions. Allaoui and Artiba (2004) studied the scheduling problem in a hybrid flow shop with both resumable and nonresumable jobs and maintenance constraints to minimize flow time and due date based criteria. Setup, cleaning and transportation times are also considered. Three dispatching rules, a simulated annealing (SA) heuristic and a flexible simulation model are separately used to solve the problem. Aggoune (2004) addressed a flow shop with machine availability constraints to minimize the makespan. Two variants of the non-preemptive constraints are considered: the starting times of maintenance activities are either fixed or flexible. An algorithm based on GA and tabu search (TS) is applied to solve the problem. Mauguiere et al. (2005) presented a new job-shop scheduling problem with machine availability constraints. The jobs can be either resumable or nonresumable depending on the unavailability period. Kubzin and Strusevich (2006) studied both a twomachine open shop problem and a two-machine flow shop problem to minimize the makespan. Each machine is subject to preventive maintenance, and the length of each maintenance period depends on its starting time. Breit (2006) investigated a problem of scheduling n preemptive jobs in a two-machine flow shop where the first machine is not available for processing during a given time interval, with the minimization of makespan. Gao, Gen, and Sun (2006) considered a flexible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP) with machine availability constraints. The periods of unavailability are non-fixed and flexible within an end-time window and have to be determined during the scheduling procedure. A hybrid genetic algorithm is proposed to solve the problem. Ruiz, Garcia-Diaz, and Maroto (2007) considered preventive maintenance and production scheduling in regular flow shops and six meta-heuristics are proposed with comparisons. The multi-purpose machine (MPM) scheduling problem with fixed machine availability constraints in a job-shop is studied in Zribi, Kamel, and Borne (2008). A two-phase heuristic method is proposed to solve the problem. In the first phase, a heuristic based on priority rules to solve the assignment problem is developed, which can be improved with a tabu search algorithm. In the second phase, a GA is presented to solve the sequencing problem. Yang, Hsu, and Kuo (2008) investigated a two-machine flow shop where maintenance activities with a constant time must be done after completing a fixed number of jobs at most. The objective is to find the optimal job combinations and the optimal job schedule to minimize the makespan. Naderi, Zandieh, and Ghomi (2009) investigated a job-shop scheduling problem with sequence-dependen set-up times and maintenance activities to minimize the makespan. Two meta-heuristics, simulated annealing (SA) and GA are used to solve the problem
Based on the previous works review mentioned above, two gains could be drawn. Firstly, most existing literature focus on the problem of integrating production scheduling with preventive maintenance activities in the context of single machine, parallel machine and flow shop (especially two-machine problems). There is much less literature in the flexible job-shop manufacturing environment. As mentioned above, Gao et al. (2006) studied the general flexible job-shop scheduling problem combined with maintenance and production. Zribi et al. (2008) considered the MPM job-shop scheduling problem with availability constraints, which is the same problem as that of Gao et al. (2006). The hybrid flow shop with availability constraints in Allaoui and Artiba (2004) is one special type of FJSP with maintenance activities. Chan, Chung, Chan, Finke, and Tiwari (2006) considered distributed flexible manufacturing system (FMS) scheduling problems subject to machine maintenance constraint, in which the maintenance time is related to the machine age. This also covers the FJSP with maintenance activities. However, as compared with the models of single machine, parallel machine and flow shop, studies dealing with the FJSP with maintenance activities are rather rare.

<sup>1</sup> Resumable means that if a job cannot be finished before a maintenance activity, it can continue the processing once the maintenance activity is finished. Nonresumable means a job must be reprocessed fully after the maintenance if its processing is interrupted by the maintenance activity on a machine. Semiresumable means that if a job is not processed to completion before the machine is stopped for maintenance, an additional set-up time is necessary when the processing is resumed.
The flexible job-shop extends the classical job-shop by overcoming the assumption of predetermining machine route and extends the classical parallel machines with multiple processing stages, to meet the real-world scenarios of production flexibility in a wide variety of products and faster production rates. The FJSP allows that a machine may be capable of performing more than one type of operation (Najib, Dauzere-Peres, & Zaidat, 2002). The FJSP at least reflects two practical scenarios such as flexible manufacturing systems (FMS) with multi-processor machines and scheduling of crane in port container terminals. The FJSP possesses two difficulties: how to assign each operation to one machine that is able to perform it (routing sub-problem) and how to determine starting times for each operation (sequencing sub-problem). Due to its significant theoretical and industrial importance, the FJSP has been explored to some extent in the literature since seminal work of Brandimarte (1993), such as Kacem, Hammadi, and Borne (2002a, 2002b), Xia and Wu (2005), Pezzella, Morganti, and Ciaschetti (2008), Gao, Sun, and Gen (2008), Wang, Zhou, and Xi (2008). Combined with the scheduling of maintenance activities and the standard FJSP provides additional complexity and new problems (Gao et al., 2006). More importantly, the integration scheduling of maintenance activities in the context of flexible job-shop environment is much more practical. Hence, it deserves further exploration to extend its theoretical significance and to explore its managerial implication.
Secondly, most existing literature consider the fixed machine availability constraint, that is, the starting time and the end time of maintenance activities are pre-determined in maintenance planning. However, in practice, preventive maintenance tasks would impose non-fixed availability constraints on the machine in that the starting time of these maintenance tasks is generally flexible (Gao et al., 2006). This means that the starting time of the unavailable periods is not known in advance and has to be determined within the given time window during the scheduling process. Currently, there is only a few works considered the non-fixed availability constraints, such as Graves and Lee (1999), Aggoune (2004), Kubzin and Strusevich (2006), Gao et al. (2006). Therefore, there is much room for further investigation.
Moreover, the constraints of maintenance resources (e.g., maintenance personnel, spare parts) should be considered. In a single machine scheduling problem with maintenance tasks, there is no need to consider this constraint since there is no conflict between maintenance resources and maintenance requirement. However, the conflict exists in the environment with multiple machines, and when only one machine can be maintained at any given time due to the limitation of maintenance resources. Lee and Chen (2000) considered the constraints of maintenance resources in parallel-machines scheduling with maintenance activities. In the FJSP with maintenance tasks discussed in Gao et al. (2006), the maintenance resource is assumed to be sufficient and the case of limited maintenance resource is not considered.
In this context, inspired by the work of Gao et al. (2006), and based on our previous work in FJSP (Wang et al., 2008), this paper proposes a heuristic based on the filtered beam search (FBS) algorithm to solve the flexible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP) with the non-fixed and fixed machine availability constraints due to the preventive maintenance, while considering two cases of maintenance resources constraints: sufficient maintenance resources or only one maintenance resource. In the first case, sufficient maintenance resources are available so that more than one machine can be maintained simultaneously if necessary. In the second case, only one machine can be maintained at any given time. A modified FBS procedure is presented to easily incorporate the machine availability constraint and the maintenance resource constraint.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the formal description of the flexible job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities. Section 3 illustrates the specific FBS procedure for the problem under investigation. In Section 4, benchmarking examples are investigated with the proposed algorithm and comparisons are presented. In Section 5, conclusions are drawn and future work directions are given.

## 2. Statement of flexible job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities
The flexible job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities that we addressed here belongs to the broad field of the deterministic scheduling with machine availability constraints, and it can be normally described as follows.
A set of n jobs is to be processed on a set of m machines denoted by $M ( M = \{ M _ { 1 } , M _ { 2 } , . ~ . ~ . , M _ { m } \} )$ . Each job $j ( 1 \leqslant j \leqslant n )$ consists of a sequence of n operations (routing). Each operation $O _ { i j } ( 1 \leqslant j \leqslant n , 1 \leqslant i \leqslant n _ { j } )$ has to be performed to complete one job. The process of each operation requires one machine out of a set $M _ { i j }$ of given machines, $M _ { i j } \subseteq M ,$ and the processing time of an operation $O _ { i j }$ on the machine M is $p _ { i j k } ( M _ { k } \in M _ { i j } \ \subseteq M )$ . There are $L _ { k } ( k = 1$ $2 , \ldots , m )$ maintenance activities $\mathsf { P M } _ { u } ^ { k } ( u \in L _ { k } )$ that have to be processed on each machine $M _ { k } c$ during the planning horizon based on a certain maintenance policy (e.g., periodical policy, sequential policy (Wang, 2002) or preventive maintenance policy in Ruiz et al. (2007)). In the case of non-fixed availability constraint, the starting time of each maintenance task is within a predefined time window $\left[ \underline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } , \overline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } \right] ( k = 1 , 2 , \ldots , m , u \in L _ { k } ) \Bigl ( \underline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } < \overline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } \Bigr )$ , and the duration of the maintenance task is pre-determined as $p m _ { u } ^ { k }$ . While in the case of fixed availability constraint, $\underline { S } _ { u } ^ { k } = \overline { S } _ { u } ^ { k }$ . The processing is nonresumable, i.e. a job must be reprocessed fully after the maintenance if its processing is interrupted by the maintenance activity on the machine.
The FJSP with maintenance activities is to determine an assignment of the operations on the machines, a sequence of the operations, and maintenance tasks on the machines that optimizes one or several criteria. In this study, the following three criteria are to be minimized
$F _ { 1 } \colon$ Makespan or maximal completion time of machines.
$F _ { 2 } \colon$ Total workload of the machines, which represents the total working time of all machines.
$F _ { 3 } \mathbf { : }$ Critical machine workload, i.e. the workload of the most loaded machine.
These three criteria were considered in literature on the standard FJSP, like Kacem et al. (2002b), Xia and Wu (2005), Wang et al. (2008). These criteria are conflicting, which is explained in our previous work of Wang et al. (2008). In this work, the maintenance periods are also included in these three criteria as Gao et al. (2006) did, because the maintenance periods are mandatory and the decision maker has to schedule the maintenance periods along with the jobs to be processed.
Assumptions considered in this paper are given in the following:
1. The jobs are non-preemptive.
S. Wang, J. Yu / Computers & Industrial Engineering 59 (2010) 436–447
2. The jobs are independent of each other and all jobs can be performed at $r _ { j }$ (release time).
3. All machines are independent of each other and are available at $t = 0 .$
4. An operation cannot be performed by more than one machine at the same time and each machine can perform only one operation at a time.
5. The set-up and removal times are sequence independent and included in the processing times or can be neglected.
6. The transportation times of operations among machines are neglected.
7. There is an unlimited in-progress product inventory, in which a job can wait for a machine until it is available.
8. There are two cases of maintenance resources constraint. One case is that there are sufficient maintenance resources such that any number of machines can be maintained or repaired simultaneously. Another case is that the maintenance resources are limited so that only one machine can be maintained at any given time and hence the maintenance activity on one machine cannot be overlapped with that of another machine.
9. When a maintenance task is performed on a machine, no operation can be processed on that machine.
10. In the planning horizon, there is at least one maintenance task on a machine. The earliest starting time and the latest starting time satisfy $\underline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } \leqslant \overline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k }$

## 3.1. Filtered beam search
Filtered beam search is an extension of beam search. Beam search is an adaptation of the branch-and-bound method in which it only explores the promising nodes level by level without backtracking. The number of nodes explored at each level is called the beamwidth. The node evaluation process at each level is a key issue in the beam search technique (Valente & Alves, 2005). An evaluation function is usually used to determine which nodes to continue the search on, which poses the problem of finding a good trade-off between quick, but poor evaluation and more computationally demanding, but better evaluation (Sabuncuoglu & Bayiz, 1999).
To find a good trade-off mentioned above economically and quickly, filtered beam search is introduced (Ow & Morton, 1988). Filtered beam search procedure uses both crude and accurate evaluations in two phases: filtering phase and beam selection phase. All nodes generated from a parent node are evaluated crudely by a computationally inexpensive filtering procedure (normally named as local evaluation function) in the first phase, leaving filterwidth filtered nodes for further accurate evaluation by a total cost evaluation function (normally named as global evaluation function) in the second phase. Those nodes found most promising are added to a partial solution. This procedure is repeated on parallel beamwidth paths until the complete schedules are reached. Hence, the number of solutions saved is equal to size of the beamwidth. Eventually, the solution with the best objective function value is as the final schedule.
As shown in Fig. 1, the promising nodes (beam nodes) are determined by applying local and global evaluation functions and proceed with the search through these selected nodes. After determining the beam nodes in level 1, the filtered beam search procedure is employed independently to generate one partial tree from each of them (in Fig. 1, there are two partial trees since beamwidth = 2). These partial trees are referred as beam paths. In each beam path, once a beam node is determined, nodes are generated in next level from this beam node by applying branching scheme. These generated nodes first subject to filtering phase, in which some of them are pruned by local evaluation and filterwidth (filterwidth = 2 in Fig. 1) filtered nodes are left for beam selection phase. Through global evaluation function, one of the filtered nodes with best global evaluation function value is determined as beam node for the level. The procedure is repeated in Fig. 1 and at last it forms two beam paths.

## 3.2. Modified FBS-based heuristic for the FJSP with maintenance tasks
The proposed heuristic is the follow up of our previous work of Wang et al. (2008). As the FBS-based heuristic algorithm for FJSP, the modified FBS-based heuristic should also solve four major elements: (1) search tree representation to define a solution space; (2) determination of beamwidth and filterwidth; (3) branching scheme; (4) local and global evaluation functions selection. Among them, (1) and (2) are defined as same as those of Wang et al. (2008).
Branching scheme is modified to incorporate with the machine availability constraint and maintenance resource constraints.
Maintenance activities can be regarded as specific production jobs. In the case of sufficient maintenance resources, each maintenance activity can be seen as a job with only one operation without any precedent constraints. While in the case of only one maintenance resource, there is a precedent constraint among maintenance activities. To adapt to the maintenance activities in the FJSP, the branching scheme is a modification form of the M\_NON-DELAY proposed in Wang et al. (2008). For differentiation, we call it MNew\_NON here.
The basic idea of the MNew\_NON is: maintenance activities are also considered as operations that should be processed only on the pre-determined machine with the earliest starting time $S _ { u } ^ { k }$ and latest starting time $\overline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } \ ( \underline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k } = \overline { { S } } _ { u } ^ { k }$ for the fixed availability constraint). The bottom line is that the period from the latest starting time plus the duration for the maintenance task $p m _ { u } ^ { k }$ should be at least reserved for the maintenance task. It is possible that the maintenance task could be processed earlier if the system overall criteria suggests based on the computation of the proposed FBSbased heuristic.

## 4.2. An example of MPM job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities
The MPM job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities is taken from Zribi et al. (2008). It is made of 15 jobs, five operations per job and five machines. Each machine is subject to two maintenance periods as follows:
M : [201,250], [463,512] means that the machine M is unavailable between 201 and 250 time units and between 463 and 512 time units. M : [104,139], [520,588], M : [233,331], [499,528], M : [137,186], [507,556], M : [129,187], [783,881]. The objective is to minimize the makespan. Zribi et al. (2008) employed a two-stage heuristic: an assignment heuristic for the assignment problem, which then could be improved by a tabu search (TS), and a genetic algorithm for the sequencing problem. With the parameters setting of genetic algorithm (population size = 200, crossover rate = 0.8, mutation rate = 0.2, selection method = wheel, generations number = 400, number of execution = 10), the schedule result with assignment heuristic and GA is 1023, and the result with assignment heuristic enhanced by TS and GA is 968.
In this paper, the problem is computed with the proposed heuristic method. The input data of the problem is shown in Fig. 11. The beamwidth $b = 7$ and filterwidth f = 7. The obtained schedule results are shown in Fig. 12 with the makespan 979. The result is much better than that of the two-stage method of assignment heuristic and $\mathsf { G A } ,$ and is very close to that of the combined method with assignment heuristic enhanced by TS and GA.

## 5. Conclusions
Production scheduling with machine availability constraints due to preventive maintenance has attracted more and more researchers, as the importance of applications is recognized. In this work, a scheduling problem with both fixed and non-fixed machine availability constraints due to maintenance activities is considered in the flexible job-shop manufacturing environment. Two cases of maintenance resources (i.e., unlimited maintenance resources and only one maintenance resource) are also considered. Thus, the extended flexible job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities is a much closer to the scheduling problems in realistic applications and possesses much more difficulties.
A heuristic based on filtered beam search (FBS) algorithm is proposed to solve this variant flexible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP) with maintenance activities and maintenance resources constraint. A modified branching scheme is provided to easily incorporate both machine availability constraints and maintenance resource constraints. In order to test the effectiveness and easiness of the proposed heuristic, two representative experimental examples extended from the standard FJSP benchmarking problems and a MPM job-shop scheduling problem with maintenance activities are tested. The results show that the proposed heuristic can obtain satisfactory solutions.
S. Wang, J. Yu / Computers & Industrial Engineering 59 (2010) 436–447
For the future work, the problem of maintenance resources optimality for the FJSP problem considering preventive maintenance with nonresumable jobs and resumable jobs in terms of manufacturing cost related performance measurement will be further investigated. Moreover, current work still belongs to the deterministic scheduling with machine availability constraints, in which maintenance activities are given as problem input data, not as a result of the machine operation (e.g., a function of machining time). Future work will also concern the jointly optimization problem considering PM policy selection, PM operations scheduling and production scheduling.

## A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem Makespan Preventive maintenance Iterated greedy algorithm Heuristic methods

## A B S T R A C T
In recent years, distributed scheduling problems have been well studied for their close connection with multifactory production networks. However, the maintenance operations that are commonly carried out on a sys tem to restore it to a specific state are seldom taken into consideration. In this paper, we study a distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with preventive maintenance operation (PM/DPFSP). A multi-start iterated greedy (MSIG) algorithm is proposed to minimize the makespan. An improved heuristic is presented for the initialization and re-initialization by adding a dropout operation to NEH2 to generate solutions with a high level of quality and disperstiveness. A destruction phase with the tournament selection and a construction phase with an enhanced strategy are introduced to avoid local optima. A local search based on three effective operators is integrated into the MSIG to reinforce local neighborhood solution exploitation. In addition. a restart strategy is adpoted if a solution has not been improved in a certain number of consecutive iterations. We con ducted extensive experiments to test the performance of the presented MSIG. The computational results indicate that the presented MSIG has many promising advantages in solving the PM/DPFSP under consideration.

## 1. Introduction
The distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem (DPFSP) has attracted increasing attention (Fernandez-Viagas & Framinan, 2015; Pan et al., 2019) in the context of decentralized and globalized economy. A multi-factory production environment is becoming more and more common. In multi-factory production network, the total manufacture tasks are allocated among serval independent units, which brings great benefits to the enterprise, including higher production efficiency, lower production costs, better product quality, and so on (Behnamian & Ghomi, 2016). The DPFSP explores the production scheduling problem under the condition that companies have established factories in different locations.
DPFSP contains n jobs in the set $N = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . , n \}$ that is to be assigned to one factory out of a set of F identical factories $G = \left\{ 1 , 2 , . . . , F \right\}$ , in which each factory contains the same series of m machines $M = \{ 1 , 2 . .$ m}. It is assumed that all the machines are continuously available from the beginning to the end in the production process. Nevertheless, in the actual industrial production, reliability and maintainability decrease as the operation time of the machine increases (Rausand & Høyland, 2003). Generally, companies are aiming at a reliable production system with high availability performance. Therefore, maintenance operations are carried out on a system to restore it to a specific state (Birolini, 2013). There are two large types of maintenance operations: corrective main tenance (CM) and preventive maintenance (PM). The actions carried out after the failure has already occurred are referred to as CM. PM opera tions are carried out on machines before the breakdown or failure takes place. The purpose of PM operations is to increase equipment life and to enhance production management during production operations. The advantage of PM is that machines are always in good condition, thus reducing the risk of failures and avoiding the loss of failure. In industry, PM operations are widely used and planned to be conducted at pre defined time intervals without considering specific working conditions of equipment.
In this paper, the DPFSP with PM operation (PM/DPFSP) is consid ered. A complete schedule of the PM/DPFSP involves two subproblems: the assignment of jobs to F factories and the sequence of jobs in each factory. The PM/DPFSP is an NP-Hard problem as a variation of DPFSF (Naderi & Ruiz, 2010). The objective is to minimize the maximum complete time $C _ { m a x }$ among all the factories. In order to obtain solutions with both good quality and high efficiency, we propose a multi-start iterated greedy (MSIG) algorithm in this paper. The MSIG is a meta heuristic algorithm that obtains only one candidate solution in each iteration. To generate an initial solution with both good quality and diversity, we apply an improved NEH2 heuristic method with dropout operations. Then in the destruction and construction phases, a few jobs are randomly removed from the current solution and then greedily reinserted into new positions to explore neighboring solutions. After ward, we consider two operators to propose three local search methods to constitute an efficient local search procedure. Finally, we utilize a simulated annealing acceptance criterion and a restart strategy to pre vent local optimum. The purpose of the restart strategy is to reinitialize the current solution after it has not been improved for serval iterations.

## 2. Literature review
The closely related literature can be divided into two categories: DPFSP and the scheduling problems with PM operation. In order to narrow the gap between academic research and practical applications, DPFSP has been studied for a long time as an extension of the permu tation flowshop scheduling problem (Maccarthy and Liu, 1993). Naderi and Ruiz (2010) first denoted DPFSP as $D P / p r m u / C _ { m a x } ,$ and proposed a total of 12 heuristic methods and two variable neighborhood descent (VND) algorithms. Following the initial work of Naderi and Ruiz (2010), many authors have studied more advanced algorithms in the last de cades. A hybrid genetic algorithm was presented by Gao and Chen (2011) to minimize the maximum completion time, where an efficient local search was utilized to explore neighboring solutions. Gao, Chen and Deng (2013) proposed a tabu algorithm with a novel tabu strategy. They utilized an enhanced local search method and a sub-sequence swapping method to generate neighborhood solutions. Lin. Ying and Huang (2013) modified the iterated greedy (IG) algorithm for the DPFSP. and proposed a destruction operator with a variable number of removed jobs and a simulated annealing algorithm with a sinking tem perature. Wang et al. (2013) proposed an effective estimation of distri. bution algorithm (EDA). They employed the earliest completion factory rule, and designed a probability model, and proposed four local search operators based on the problem characteristics. Naderi and Ruiz (2014) presented a scatter search (SS) procedure, which has seldom been explored for flowshop settings. The SS procedure was demonstrated to statistically outperform the other 11 algorithms in the experiments. Xu et al. (201 4) proposed a hybrid immune algorithm, where four different local search operators were used in a hybrid way within the frame of the immune algorithm. Fernandez-Viagas and Framinan (2015) developed a bounded-search IG algorithm for the DPESP In order to reduce the number of solutions to be evaluated. they studied the property of the problem to estimate the makespan of a factory when a new job is inserted. The effect of the bounded search method is that the compu tational time is discarded by 32.31% and the number of iterations is decreased by 11.68%. Bargaoui, Belkahla Driss and Gh´edira (2017) presented a chemical reaction optimization algorithm, in which a one point crossover and a greedy strategy are embedded to ameliorate the solution quality. Deng and Wang (2017) proposed a competitive mem: etic algorithm to solve the multi-objective DPFSP with makespan and total tardiness criteria. They employed two populations to optimize the two objectives and designed the interaction between the two pop ulations to balance the two obiectives. Ruiz. Pan and Naderi (2019) presented a simple two-stage iterated greedy (IG2S) algorithm with improved initialization, destruction, construction and local search procedures. Despite its simplicity, the IG2S significantly exceeds the other state-of-the-art algorithms in comparison. For the DPFSP with total flowtime optimization, Fernandezviagas, Perezgonzalez and Fra minan (2018) proposed eighteen constructive heuristics to generate feasible solutions with high quality in reasonable computational time and an evolutionary algorithm to further improve the so-obtained so lutions. Pan et al. (2019) Introduced three constructive heuristics and four metaheuristics to suit the needs of different CPU time demands and solution quality.
There are also literatures proposed for other variations of the DPFSP. Rifai, Nguyen and Dawal (2016) gave a survey of the distributed reen trant permutation flowshop scheduling problem and developed a multiobjective adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm. Wang and Wang (2016) proposed a memetic algorithm for solving the distributed assembly permutation flowshop. Wang, Huang and Qin (2016) consid ered the DPFSP under machine breakdown with makespan criterion and proposed a fuzzy logic-based hybrid EDA. Zhang, Xing and Cao (2018) presented a hybrid discrete differential evolution (DDE) algorithm to deal with the distributed blocking flowshop scheduling problem (DBFSP) with makespan criterion. Pan et al. (2019) addressed a distributed assembly permutation flowshop scheduling problem in which each factory consists of a flowshop for part-processing and an assembly line for product-processing. Meng, Pan and Wang (2019) studied a DPFSP with customer order constraint. Jing et al. (2020) dealt with the DPFSP with due windows to minimize the total weighted earliness and tardiness. Huang, Pan and Gao (2020) extend the DPFSP by considering the sequence-dependent setup time (SDST). Zhao et al. (2020) presented an ensemble DDE algorithm for solving the DBFSP with makespan minimization. Meng and Pan (2021) solved a DPFSP with non-identical factories (DPFSP-NF) with lot-streaming and SDST considered. Lu et al. (2021) presented a knowledge-based multi-objec tive memetic optimization algorithm to minimizing makespan, negative social impact and total energy consumption of the DPFSP-NF. Wang and Wang (2020) applied a knowledge-based cooperative algorithm to address the energy-efficient scheduling of the DPFSP. Most recently, Huang et al. (2021) proposed three heuristic methods and an effective DABC algorithm for minimizing the makespan of the DPFSP with the machine-independent SDST.
The corresponding literatures on the scheduling problem with PM operation are abundant as well. Ruiz, Garciadiaz and Maroto (2007) considered PM operation in a flowshop scheduling problem. They compared three PM policies and tested three heuristics and two meta heuristic methods. Extensive computational evaluations have given a result that the genetic algorithm (GA) and the ant colony optimization algorithm (ACO) are the two best algorithms. Yang, Hsu and Kuo (2008) considered a two-machine flowshop scheduling problem with a sepa rated maintenance constraint. According to their problem, the machine needs PM operations after it completes a certain amount of jobs rather than keeps working for a certain period of time. Wang and Yu (2010) proposed a filtered beam search based heuristic algorithm for solving a flexible job-shop scheduling problem with machine availability con straints. They studied a scheduling problem with both fixed and non fixed machine availability constraints in the flexible job-shop manufacturing environment. Naderi, Zandieh and Amimmayeri (2011) investigated a flexible flowshop scheduling with periodic PM operation on machines to minimize makespan. They applied a GA and an artificial immune system to solve the problem. Wong, Chan and Chung (2013) formulated a new scheduling problem with multiple resources and PM tasks as an integer-programming model and solved it by a GA approach. Xu and Yang (2013) studied a two-parallel-machines scheduling prob lem where one machine is periodically unavailable and jobs are nonpreemptive. They applied the classical longest processing time first (LPT) rule and the list scheduling (LS) rule for minimizing the makespan. Computational experiments showed that the LPT beat the LS. Lei and Liu (2020) applied an artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm with a division for solving distributed unrelated parallel machines scheduling problems with PM operations. To generate solutions with high quality, they divided the whole swarm into one employed bee colony and three onlooker bee colonies, whose search strategy were different from each other.

As has been reviewed above, the DPFSP and the scheduling problems with PM operations have been widely studied in recent years. To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing literature on PM/DPFSP. Even though many high-performance algorithms have been developed, we are not aware of how well these existing algorithms perform on the PM/ DPFSP. ## 3. DPFSP with PM operation The PM/DPFSP can be depicted as follows. The set of jobs N is to be assigned to the factory set G. In each factory, all the jobs are processed on the machine set M in the order from machine 1 to machine m following the same route. Each machine i, i M, can only process one job simultaneously and each job $j , j \in N ,$ , can only be processed on one machine at one time. Each job j requires a certain amount of processing time on each machine $i ,$ which is described as $p _ { i , j } .$ All the jobs and ma chines are available for the process at time 0. In order to ensure the maintainability and reliability of a production system, PM operations are processed on all the machines periodically. The maintenance oper ation performed on machine i is described as $P M _ { i } , i \in M .$ The processing interval of PM is denoted as $I _ { i } ,$ which means that for each I units of processing time, machine i must be stopped for PM. The processing time of PM is denoted as $T _ { i \cdot }$ Once a job or a PM operation starts its processing on a machine, it cannot be interrupted. The following example illustrates a solution of PM/DPFSP. Suppose that there is a set of ten jobs to be assigned to two factories each of which consists of two machines, that is, $m = 3 , n = 1 0$ and F = 2. The processing time of the jobs and PM operations are shown in Table 1. Fig. 1 shows an optimal solution for the example without considering the PM operator, i.e. the original DPFSP. We obtain the optimal solu tions by enumerating all the feasible solutions. One of them ${ \mathrm { i } } s ,$ the job sequences at factory 0 and factory 1 being {8, 3, 4, 7, 1} and {6, 9, 3, 5, 0} respectively. The makespan of this solution is 36. In Fig. 2, the scheduling criterion of the PM operations is applied to the previous optimal solution. It can be seen that the PM operations disrupted the tight schedule. There is plenty of idle time on machine 2 in each factory, which leads to larger completion time. Take job 2 in factory 1 on ma chine 1 for example to illustrate the PM operation, the accumulated total processing time before job 2 starts is $p _ { 1 , 6 } + p _ { 1 , 9 } = 2 + 2 = 4 ,$ which is no larger than the interval time of PM operations on machine 2. While job 2 has a processing time of $p _ { 1 , 2 } = 9$ on machine 1, resulting in an accu mulated total processing time of 13 units, which is above $\mathrm { I } _ { 1 } \ = \ 9 .$ Therefore, a PM operation is performed following job 2 on machine 1. The processing of job 5 is suspended until the PM operation finishes at time 32. Meanwhile, the accumulated total processing time on machine 1 is reset after maintenance. The same rule is applied to all the machines, thus producing makespan of 64. Fig. 3 shows the Gantt chart for a solution to the previous problem but taking PM operations into consideration during scheduling. The solution consists of a job sequence {8, 6, 3, 7, 1} in factory 0 and a job sequence {4, 9, 2, 0, 5} in factory 1. As we can see, the new solution of the optimization has less idle time and fewer PM operations. In addition, the makespan is now 51, which implies a decrease in the initial solution in Fig. 2 of 20.3%. The explanation is given by the fact that the solution with PM operations considered is usually different from the one if the PM operations are not considered (Ruiz et al., 2007). ## 4. The proposed multi-start iterated greedy algorithm In the literature, a high performing heuristic is often used to initialize the search for an IG algorithm. The main loop is to greedily repeat four operations (Ruiz & Stützle, 2007; Ruiz, Pan & Naderi, 2019): Utilize the destruction to partially destroy the candidate solution. For our problem, some jobs will be removed from the solution, resulting in an incomplete solution and a group of leftover jobs. Apply a greedy heuristic method to reinsert the removed jobs into the solution. A new complete solution will be generated in this con struction phase. ## 4.1. Solution representation To represent the job assignment to factories, a solution is represented by a two-dimensional array $\Pi = \{ \pi \sb { 1 } , \pi \sb { 2 } , . . . , \pi _ { F } \}$ }. There are F rows in the array, in which each row has a job sequence $\pi _ { f } ( f = 1 , 2 , . . . , F )$ consisting of a set of jobs assigned to the factory. Jobs in each sequence are sorted according to the processing order. For instance, the solution as shown in Fig. 3 can be represented as Π = {(8, 6, 3, 7, 1), (4, 9, 2, 0, 5)}. According to the PM strategy we take, once job sequences are determined, starting and ending times of PM operations on all machines are also fixed. So, there is no need to record PM operations in π . Such a sequence-based solution is widely used in the scheduling literature for its intuitive representation and convenience for programming (Arroyo, Leung & Tavares, 2019). ## 4.2. Heuristic method As for the initialization procedure, we propose an improved NEH2 heuristic method with dropout operation (INEH2\_dp for short) to pro duce a solution with a high level of quality. The NEH algorithm of Nawaz, Enscore and Ham (1983) has been regarded to be one of the most effective heuristic algorithms for the permutation flowshop scheduling problem (PFSP) with the makespan criterion (Ruiz & Maroto, 2005). Naderi and Ruiz (2010) extended NEH by considering the allocation of jobs to factories to fit for DPFSP and proposed the NEH1 and NEH2. The NEH2\_en of Ruiz, Pan and Naderi (2019) is a further improvement on the NEH2 method which increases the computational complexity to obtain a better performance. In the NEH2, all the jobs are first arranged in decreasing order of the total processing time on m machines $P _ { j } =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } p _ { i , j } , \forall j \in N , } \end{array}$ resulting in the largest processing time (LPT) sequence. Then the jobs are orderly taken out from the sequence and placed at the best positions among all the F factories. The NEH2\_en improved the NEH2 heuristic in which after the position of a new job is fixed, either the job on its predecessor or successor is extracted at random and reinserted in the best positions in the same factory. Inspired by the NEH2\_en, we propose the INEH2\_dp method to fit our problem. The pseudo codes of INEH2\_dp are given in Fig. 4.

In our INEH2\_dp heuristic method, the new job taken out from the LPT sequence is not greedily tested in all the positions in all the factories. Instead, each possible position has a certain probability k of being ignored. We refer to this operator and its probability k as dropout and dropout rate, where k is a parameter to be calibrated. The purpose of the dropout operator is to enhance some stochastics to our heuristic so that a different initial solution with a high level of quality can be generated when the algorithm restarts. In addition, the predecessor and successor of the inserted job are compared by $P _ { j } .$ We select the job with a smaller P and test to swap it with all the other jobs in the same factory. Finally, the swapping operator producing the least makespan is chosen. In the course of $C _ { m a x }$ calculation, each job on each machine in the sequence $\pi _ { f }$ is traversed one by one. There is an average of n/F jobs in each factory. This makes the complexity of $C _ { m a x }$ calculation in one fac tory equal to O(nm/F). INEH2\_dp evaluates a total of $[ n ( n + F ) / 2 ] { - } F$ schedules, which obtains the complexity of O(n3m/F). Note that the dropout operator does not change the framework of the proposed heu ristic, so it does not reduce the theoretical complexity.

Construction phase As for the construction, we recombine the temporary sequence $\lambda _ { d }$ and the remaining partial solution π to reconstruct a new complete candidate solution. We found that the previously mentioned heuristic method can obtain good results with a little modification. Jobs in $\lambda _ { d }$ are rearranged by the total processing time $P _ { j } .$ We greedily insert the jobs into the best position among all the factories in the order of $P _ { j } ,$ from the largest to the smallest. Unlike in the INEH2\_dp, where the selected predecessor or successor is tested to swap with jobs in the corresponding factory, the construction operator tests to swap the selected job with all the jobs in all the factories. It is assumed that each factory has an average of n/F jobs, so the complexity of testing to insert one job into all the possible positions and to swap one job with all the jobs are both O(n2m/F). The complexity of the construction phase is O(n2md/F). The pseudo codes of construction phases are given in Fig. 6.

## 4.5. Local search methods After the destruction and construction phases, a local search is per formed to further improve the solution. As to the permutation-based neighborhood structure, the swap and insertion operators are widely used in the local search phase (Fernandezviagas, Valente & Framinan, 2018). The swap operator is to interchange the positions of two jobs. The insertion operator removes a job from its original position and reinserts it into a different position. Based on the two operators, we propose three effective local search methods for the PM/DPFSP. The pseudo codes of the three local search methods are presented in Figs. 7–9, respectively. Inter-factory Swap Local Search (ISLS): We test to swap each job in each factory in random order with the other jobs in the same factory. If an improvement swap is carried out, or all tests in a factory are completed, we end the search in the factory and begins the search in the next one. In the worst case where the solution is not improved, (n/F)(n/ F− 1)/2 swap operations will be tested in each factory. The ISLS termi nates after all the factories get the swap search done. Therefore, the complexity of the ISLS in all F factories is O(n3m/F2). External-key-factory Swap Local Search (ESLS): In the PM/DPFSP, it is noted that makespan is determined by the factory with the largest makespan. Such a factory is referred to as the key factory, denoted as $f _ { k e y } .$ Jobs in $f _ { k e y }$ are picked up in a random order without repetition. Then we test to swap the selected job with all the other jobs in all the factories (including $f _ { k e y } )$ and then perform the best swap with the lowest $C _ { m a x } .$ The procedure terminates if an improvement is achieved, or all the jobs in $f _ { k e y }$ have been tested. It is assumed that there are averagely n/F jobs in $f _ { k e y } ,$ so $n ^ { 2 } / F$ swap operations will be tested at most. The complexity of ESLS is $O ( n ^ { 3 } m / \bar { F } ^ { 2 } )$ . External-key-factory Insertion Local Search (EILS): Similar to the ESLL, the EILS tests to reinsert jobs in $f _ { k e y }$ in all the factories (including $f _ { k e y } )$ and conduct the best insertion in order to minimize the $C _ { m a x } .$ . Unlike ESLS, in which test of swapping jobs in two factories generates two new solutions and needs to calculate $C _ { m a x }$ result twice, the EILS only calcu lates one $C _ { m a x }$ result. Therefore, EILS shares the same complexity of O $( n ^ { 3 } m / F ^ { 2 } )$ with ESLS but theoretically has shorter computation time. The local search phase is composed of the three proposed local search methods. It repeatedly calls the ISLS, the ESLS and the EILS until no better solution can be obtained. The pseudo codes of the complete local search procedures are presented in Fig. 10. ## 4.6. Acceptance criterion and restart strategy The acceptance criterion is designed to avoid local best solutions. After the destruction and construction phases and the local search phase, we apply a simulated annealing-like algorithm with constant tempera ture as an acceptance criterion. As is shown in the formula, a new so lution Π\* with a worse result than the current solution Π has a certain probability p to be accepted, so it is hopeful to abandon a local best solution and keep searching for better results. The constant temperature is based on the particular instance and it is computed following the formula suggested by Osman and Potts (1989). Despite of its simplicity, such an acceptance criterion has been widely used in scheduling prob lems (Pan et al., 2019; Ruiz & Stützle, 2007; Ruiz, Pan & Naderi, 2019). J.-y. Mao et al. Experimental results In order to evaluate the algorithmic performance, we conducted numerical experiments. To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing instance of our problem. Therefore, we generated benchmarks based on the following parameters in Table 2. The value of $n ,$ m, F and $P _ { j o b }$ are set based on the studies of Taillard (1993) and Pan et al. (2019) to cover the instances of all the scales. We also referred to Ruiz et al. (2007) to set up parameters for the PM operation. The minimum value of T is set as 50 in case too short PM operation time has little impact on scheduling. The mean value of TPM is two times of that of the average $P _ { j o b } .$ . Meanwhile, in order to simplify the problem, the range of I is set 50% to 75% of the average total pro cessing time on each machine, so that only one PM operation is carried out on each machine during the whole manufacturing process. In total. there are 45 different combinations of the number of factories $F ,$ the number of machines m and the number of jobs n. Each combination randomly generates five different instances, which results in $4 5 \times 5 = 2 2 5$ instances of varying scales. We have coded all the al gorithms in $^ { \mathrm { C + + } }$ and compiled with Visual Studio 2019 with the x64 compiler with all optimization flags enable. All the experiments in this paper are performed on Windows Server 2012 on a PC with a Quad-core processor Intel E5-2640 2.4 GHz and 4 GB of RAM. The results of all the algorithms are measured by the relative percentage deviation (RPD) (Naderi & Ruiz, 2010; Ruiz & Stützle, 2007; Ruiz et al., 2007) and it is calculated as follows: $$ RPD = 100 \% \times \frac{Some_{sol} - Best_{sol}}{Best_{sol}}\tag{3} $$ where $S o m e _ { s o l }$ is the $C _ { m a x }$ obtained by a certain algorithm on a given instance and $B e s t _ { s o l }$ is the minimum $C _ { m a x }$ found in any experiment for the same instance. We carried out an analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine whether the PRD results obtained by each algorithm are indeed significantly different. A 95% confidence level is employed in our experiments.

## 5.2. Comparison of proposed algorithms
To validate the performance of the proposed MSIG, we compared it against six state-of-the-art algorithms from the literature. These are: discrete differential evolution (DDE) algorithm (Zhang, Xing & Cao, 2018), hybrid genetic algorithm (HGA) (Huang et al., 2019), two stage iterated greedy (IG2S) algorithm (Ruiz, Pan & Naderi, 2019), iterated cocktail greedy (ICG) algorithm (Lin & Ying, 2016), improved discrete artificial bee colony (IDABC) algorithm (Mao et al., 2020a) and iterated greedy (IG) (Mao et al., 2020b) algorithm, where DDE, HGA, IG2S and ICG are not designed for PM/DPFSP, so we reconstruct them for our problem. Parameters of all algorithms are calibrated as done in MSIG and summarized in Table 4. According to the above literature, the three population-based algorithms (DDE, HGA and IDABC) and the three iteration-based algorithms (IG2S, ICG and IG) respectively possess excellent global exploration and outstanding local exploitation. There fore, they are selected to verify the proposed MSIG.
We perform five dependent runs for each algorithm to solve each of the 225 benchmarks with a given stop criterion t = 50 × m × n milli seconds. The average RPD of each instance size F|m|n is reported in Table 5. We also group the RPD values according to F, m and n in Table 6.
It can be clearly observed in Table 5 that the proposed MSIG per forms best among all the algorithms in comparison. The overall RPD values of all the algorithms, from the smallest to the largest, are respectively 0.225% of MSIG, 0.414% of IG, 0.553% of IDABC, 0.708% of IG2S, 0.768% of HGA, 3.409% of DDE and 3.492% of ICG. DDE and ICG perform much worse than the other algorithms. The bad results obtained by DDE and ICG can be explained by the lack of an effective local search mechanism. In addition, the MSIG performs best on 29 out of 45 instance sizes, which is far more than the 12 of IDABC, the seven of IG and the one of HGA. Table 6 illustrates that the MSIG obtains the best result for almost all the groups with regarding to different numbers of factories F, different numbers of machines m and different numbers of jobs n, except for n = 100, in which average RPD of IG is slightly smaller

In addition, Table 7 concludes a t-test with a significance level equal to 5% for all the results yielded by each pair of the algorithms. According to Table 7, it is clear that there is no significant difference between the pair of HGA and IG2S and the pair of DDE and ICG. All the other algo rithm pairs generate significantly different results. Therefore, we can divide the algorithms into five homogenous groups, with no significant differences within each group. In order of average RPD values, from the smallest to the largest, the groups are sorted as follows: {MSIG}, {IG}, {IDABC}, {IG2S, HGA}, and {DDE, ICG}.
In Fig. 13, we count the number of best solutions of each instance obtained by each algorithm. It can be observed that the MSIG generates the most number of best solutions among all the competitive algorithms. There are 146 best solutions generated by MSIG out of a total of 225 instances. Though IG is significantly better than IDABC in terms of average RPD results, they are tied for second place with 68 best solu tions. IG2S, HGA, DDE and ICG generate 36, 31, 8 and 8 best solutions respectively.
Fig. 14 shows the average RPD values generated by all the algorithms at the elapsed CPU time $t = 5 0 \times m \times n$ milliseconds. We record the makespan of the best solution over a period of $5 \times m \times 1$ n milliseconds to provide an overall picture of the algorithms. Meanwhile, following Zou et al. (Zou et al., 2020) and many others, a multifactor ANOVA is carried out to confirm whether the RPD values of each algorithm at each moment are indeed significantly different. As can be seen, the mean plots show that the proposed MSIG performs significantly better than the other algorithms all the time throughout the progress. DDE and ICG have the worst optimizations of all the algorithms because their RPD results are the largest and decrease very little as computational time increases. Furthermore, DDE and ICG have more parameters than the others, which increases calibration complexity. IG performs a bit worse than IDABC at the beginning, but it statistically exceeds IDABC after 35 × m × n milliseconds and further expands the gap between them as time goes on. Throughout the whole process, there is no significant difference between the RPD results of HGA and IG2S.
Next, we plot the interactions of algorithms type and the parameters of instances $F ,$ m and n in Figs. 15 and 16 based on the RPD results at t = $5 0 \times m \times n$ milliseconds. The results are again analyzed by ANOVA where $F , m ,$ and n are considered as non-controllable factors. DDE and ICG are removed from these plots as they are clearly worse than the other algorithms. We can see that when the number of factories F and the number of machines m change, the average RPD values of each algo rithm have the same changing trend, while the MSIG has the minimum variation. In other words, it is proved that MSIG has better robustness for the instances of a different scale than the other competitive algorithms. Fig. 16 shows that the population-based algorithms, HGA and IDABC, perform relatively poorly in the small-scale n of the instances while get better rapidly as n increases. When n increases to 500, HGA gains no significantly worse RPD results than the overall second-best IG. And IDABC even far exceeds IG. By contrast, the greedy iteration-based al gorithms, MSIG, IG and IG2S, generate more stable RPD results when n changes. In general, the proposed MSIG is superior to the other compared algorithms in terms of both RPD results and stability when the parameters of instances change.
Finally, it can be safely summarized that the MSIG is the most effective algorithm for solving the PM/DPFSP with makespan criterion among all the compared algorithms. The MSIG outperforms the other algorithms in terms of both RPD results and robustness.

## 6. Conclusions and future research
Distributed scheduling in multi-factory production has been a hot research topic in the past decades. However, scheduling problems with PM operations are seldom investigated. In this study, the distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with preventive maintenance (PM/DPFSP) is considered. We proposed a simple but effective multistart iterated greedy (MSIG) to minimize the makespan. The MSIG uses an improved NEH2 heuristic algorithm with a dropout operation to initialize the solution. After that, destruction and construction phases are greedily iterated. During the destruction phase, a couple of jobs are removed from the complete candidate solution. After that, the con struction phase applies a constructive heuristic to reconstruct the solu tion. In attempting to obtain optimal solutions, a local search basing on insertion and swap operations is also presented. Once a feasible solution is completed, an acceptance criterion determines whether the incum bent solution will be replaced by the new one. In addition, a solution will be abandon after a certain number of iterations without improvement. Then the algorithm restarts with the heuristic method. We carried out experiments based on randomly generated instances to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed MSIG. The experimental results have indicated that the MSIG performs much better than the existing algo rithms in the literature.
In the near future, we will still focus on PM/DPFSP. Despite the avoidance of the remaining local optima, the multi-start strategy does not take full advantage of existing solutions. We are going to further study the restarting method to promote efficiency. In addition, we are also interested in other objectives in PM/DPFSP (e.g. total flow time, total tardiness) which are common in practice.

# A Feedback Learning-Based Memetic Algorithm for Energy-Aware Distributed Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling With Transportation Constraints
Jingjing Wang , Honggui Han , Senior Member, IEEE, and Ling Wang , Member, IEEE
Abstract—With increasing energy concerns and development of globalization, energy-aware scheduling and distributed scheduling have become significant topics in modern manufacturing. However, realistic manufacturing scenarios, such as collaborative scheduling of distributed shops and limited transportation resources, are rarely taken into account. To bridge the gap, this article addresses the energy-aware distributed flexible jobshop with transportation constraints (EDFJSP-T) and proposes a feedback learning-based memetic algorithm (FLMA) to minimize makespan and total energy consumption simultaneously. First, a mathematical model is formulated to represent the relationship between different subproblems. Additionally, an encoding and decoding method based on forward insertion is designed to reduce the search space and obtain high-quality schedules. Second, various problem-specific operators are designed to focus on different subproblems and objectives to enrich search patterns. Third, memetic search with feedback learning is proposed via introducing observer indexes for both population state and individual state to adaptively match appropriate operators for individuals. Besides, local intensification search with multiple operators is incorporated for low-density regions to further improve exploitation ability. The parameter setting is investigated and experimental tests are carried out using different types of instances. The comparisons demonstrate the effectiveness of the feedback learning mechanism and the superiority of the FLMA over existing algorithms for solving the EDFJSP-T.
Index Terms—Distributed collaborative scheduling, energyaware scheduling, feedback learning, flexible job-shop, memetic algorithm (MA), transportation constraints.

## I. INTRODUCTION
REEN manufacturing is a sustainable manufacturing both economic and environmental objectives. It aims to apply the green concept to the whole life cycle of products for reducing the adverse effects on the environment and improving resource utilization [1]. Facing increasingly serious environmental issues and energy shortages, many industries pay growing attention to energy consumption (EC) during production. Production scheduling is an effective means to improve product quality and production efficiency and reduce costs and consumption without equipment upgrades and product redesign [2]. Thus, it is of extraordinary significance to develop effective energy-aware scheduling for production systems [3].
Cooperation between enterprises and industries is becoming widespread as a result of growing globalization for mutual benefit. The traditional centralized organization has been changing to multiple decentralized workshops to form distributed manufacturing mode, which has become an important modern manufacturing paradigm [4]. In distributed manufacturing, the products are produced through resource sharing and cooperation among different workshops to improve production efficiency and reduce management risks [5]. Under distributed manufacturing environment, distributed scheduling can optimize the scheduling objectives by reasonable job allocation and processing sequence. Due to its multiple subproblems and multiobjective characteristics, energy-aware distributed shop scheduling is more difficult to solve than traditional shop scheduling. Thus, it is of extraordinary significance to design effective and efficient solution algorithms for energyaware distributed shop scheduling.
As one of the classical scheduling problems, flexible jobshop scheduling problem (FJSP) has attracted attention of many researchers and widely existed in numerous practical production scenarios, such as textile production process, equipment manufacturing, chemical materials processing, and automobile assembly [6], [7], [8], [9]. As an extension of the FJSP under distributed manufacturing, the DFJSP is more complex and difficult to solve than the FJSP, since it contains three subproblems, i.e., factory assignment, machine assignment, and job sequencing. Giovanni and Pezzella [8] proposed an improved genetic algorithm (GA) with a new local searchbased operator to refine promising solutions for solving the DFJSP with makespan minimization. Meng et al. [9] proposed four mixed integer linear programming (MILP) models as well as a constraint programming (CP) model based on interval decision variables and domain filtering algorithms to obtain the optimality for 62 benchmark problems. To compare the effect of different chromosome representations for solving the DFJSP, Wu et al. [10] developed a new chromosome representation and investigated the importance of appropriate chromosome representations. For the practical distributed sand casting job-shop scheduling problem, Tang et al. [11] proposed a hybrid teaching and learning-based optimization algorithm adopting dynamic teacher group and tabu search to improve the quality of teachers.
