## D. Energy Saving Strategy In the context of scheduling problems with consideration of energy consumption, the total energy consumption is a critical metric that significantly impacts the achievement of green scheduling. One principal method for reducing energy consumption during the production of jobs is to minimize both machine processing time and idle time. In accordance with this principle, an energy-saving strategy has been devised which places an emphasis on local optimization and the modification of production sequences with a view to reducing idle time on machines and, consequently, lowering overall energy consumption throughout the production process. The strategy is based on the following principles: 1) local optimization: the application of local search techniques is utilized for the optimization of operational sequencing on machinery, with the objective of minimizing downtime and enhancing machine utilization; 2) adjusting production sequences: the reordering of operations or the adjustment of their start times may be employed to more effectively utilize machine capacity and reduce periods of inactivity; and 3) reduction of idle time: the objective is to identify and reduce instances of idle time between operations, thereby reducing unnecessary energy consumption. As shown in Fig. 3, operation $O _ { 3 1 }$ on machine M2 must wait until operation $O _ { 2 2 }$ is completed before commencing, while operation $O _ { 3 2 }$ on M1 must wait for operation $O _ { 2 3 }$ to finish before starting, resulting in significant idle time. Under the premise of maintaining scheduling constraints, shifting operation $O _ { 3 1 }$ on M2 before $O _ { 2 2 }$ and moving operation $O _ { 3 2 }$ on M1 before $O _ { 2 3 }$ can reduce machine idle time, thereby lowering idle energy consumption and shortening the completion time of jobs. This strategy, which entails maintaining the sequence of operations while rearranging the production order of different jobs, has the effect of minimizing machine idle periods. Without modifying the critical path, it contributes to a reduction in overall energy consumption and an enhancement in production efficiency. ## E. Operator Selection Based on D3QN The 12 local search operators in Table I are each suited to different optimization scenarios and optimal solutions. In the local search phase of population evolution, when optimizing the Pareto front solution, the optimal strategy needs to be dynamically selected from 12 operators. To this end, this section proposes a D3QN-based operator selection mechanism, which is invoked in the nondominated solution optimization phase of each iteration (Algorithm 3, line 25), and achieves adaptive matching of operators through deep reinforcement learning. The DQN algorithm [19] is an efficient unsupervised deep reinforcement learning algorithm capable of autonomously learning the data distribution within the solution space. In light of these distribution characteristics, a probability mapping related to operator selection is constructed. The original DQN algorithm is prone to overestimating Q-values in certain cases, which can result in instability and a decline in performance during the learning process. To address this issue, an improved version, known as double DQN (DDQN), was proposed. DDQN introduces two neural networks: one for selecting actions and computing target Q-values (referred to as the prediction network), and another for evaluating target Q-values (known as the target network). During the training phase, the target network is periodically updated to generate target Q-values in lieu of utilizing Q-values directly from the prediction network. This approach mitigates the potential for overestimation. (20) The Q-value, represented by $Q ( s , a )$ , is an implicit indication of the value associated with being in state s and the advantage gained from selecting action a. In response to this, the Dueling network [20] was developed with the explicit objective of segregating the state value and action advantage components within a given state. In the context of the dueling network framework, two distinct networks are employed with the objective of estimating the state value function, $V ( s )$ , and the action advantage function, $A ( s , a )$ , for each state. Subsequently, the action value function $Q ( s , \ a )$ is derived by integrating the aforementioned networks, as illustrated in the following equation: $$ \begin{array}{l} Q (s, a; \theta , \alpha , \beta) = V (s; \theta , \beta) \\ \qquad + \left(A (s, a; \theta , \alpha) - \frac {1}{| A |} \sum_ {a ^ {\prime}} A (s, a ^ {\prime}; \theta , \alpha)\right). \end{array}\tag{21} $$ Fig. 4 illustrates the network architecture of the D3QN, depicting how the state inputs are processed through the hidden layers to generate action values, highlighting the separation of state value and action advantage branches in the dueling network design. The D3QN network consists of an input layer, three fully connected layers (with 64, 128, and 64 neurons, respectively, all using the ReLU activation function), a branching fully connected layer (split into the value stream and advantage stream), and an output layer. State design: The local search operators are recommended based on the current job shop state, making accurate extraction and representation of this state crucial. Considering the study’s constraints related to time and energy consumption, three metrics relevant to the overall scheduling problem (number ofjobs, number of machines, total number of operations), four metrics related to job shop processing time (total machine completion time, machine idle/processing time, total completion time per factory, machine idle/processing time per factory), and two metrics related to energy consumption (total machine energy consumption, energy consumption per factory) are proposed to accurately characterize the current job shop state. ## F. D3QN-NSGA-II Algorithm Flow Sections II-A to II-E provided a detailed introduction to the main components of the D3QN-NSGA-II algorithm. Initially, the algorithm initializes parameters including population size, scaling parameter $\beta ,$ crossover probability $P _ { c } ,$ mutation probability $P _ { m } ,$ , and sets up the D3QN network. Subsequently, using the NSGA-II algorithm, the population undergoes rapid nondominated sorting and crowding distance calculation. It employs a reproductive capacity assessment mechanism to split the population based on the scaling parameter $\beta ,$ and through a dual-population evolution strategy and energy-saving scheduling strategy, it obtains a new generation of the population. The nondominated solutions from the latest generation are stored in PF. Each member of the PF population undergoes selection of a local search operator, and the resultant solution from executing this operator is compared against the original solution to ascertain its reward. During each decision-making round, the current state $S _ { t }$ , action chosen under this state $A _ { t } ,$ obtained reward $R _ { t }$ , and the next state $S _ { t + 1 }$ are combined to form experiences stored in the experience pool. If the experience pool reaches a predefined threshold, the DQN network is trained. The framework of the D3QN-NSGA-II algorithm is illustrated in Algorithm 3. ## IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETTING AND RESULTS ## A. Experimental Parameters In order to validate the effectiveness of D3QN-NSGA-II, this section employs the use of 20 test cases, as provided in the relevant literature [21]. These cases cover ranges for the number of jobs $\mathrm { n } \in \ \{ 1 0 \}$ , 20, 30, 40, 50, 100, 150, 200} and the number of factories ${ n _ { f } } \in \{ 2 , \ 3 , \ 4 , \ 5 , \ 6 , \ 7 \}$ . Each factory is comprised of five machines, and each job is comprised of five operations. The selection of machines for each operation allows for the consideration of multiple options, with processing times varying according to the specific factory and machine chosen. All machines have a processing power $W _ { P } = 4$ and an idle power $W _ { s } = 1$ . To analyze the distribution and convergence of solution sets obtained by the proposed algorithm and comparative algorithms, the hypervolume(HV) metric [22] and the inverted generational distance (IGD) are introduced. A higher HV is indicative of superior overall algorithmic performance, whereas a smaller IGD is indicative of superior convergence and distribution characteristics. Comparative algorithms include classical multiobjective optimization algorithms such as MOEA/D and several state-of-the-art swarm intelligence optimization algorithms like MOPSO [23], NSWOA [24], and MOGWO [25]. ## B. Parameter Validation The efficacy of an algorithm is significantly influenced by its key parameters. Prior to conducting simulation experiments, it is of paramount importance to validate and optimize the parameters for both the proposed algorithm and the selected comparative algorithms. To ensure fairness and consistency in the comparison, all algorithms (including MOEA/D, MOPSO, NSWOA, and MOGWO) adopt the same Taguchi method for parameter tuning, which is used to assess the impact of various parameters on algorithm performance and obtain optimal parameter combinations. The experiments are conducted based on the 20J3F test case, where each parameter combination is independently run ten times, and the results of the parameter validation are presented in Table II. For comparative algorithms, parameters were not directly adopted from original literature but retuned specifically for the DHFJS problem in this study, following the same Taguchi method framework as D3QN-NSGA-II to ensure comparable experimental conditions.

## C. Component Separation Experiment To assess the contribution of each component in the proposed strategy, we designed a comparative experiment to evaluate the effects of the dual-population evolutionary strategy, energy-efficient scheduling strategy, and D3QN-based operator selection mechanism on algorithm performance. The experiment compared the basic NSGA-II algorithm, NSGA-II with only the dual-population evolutionary strategy (DP+NSGA-II), NSGA-II with only the energy-efficient scheduling strategy (ES+NSGA-II), NSGA-II with only the D3QN-based operator selection mechanism (D3QN+NSGA-II), and the complete algorithm (D3QN-NSGA-II). To ensure the reliability of the experimental results, identical parameter settings were used for all the algorithms, and each variant was run ten times across 20 test cases to compute the average performance. This study employed SPASSAU software to analyze the significance of the relationships between algorithm variants, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed improved operators. ## D. Comparative Experiments
To provide a comprehensive assessment of the proposed algorithm’s overall performance, it was benchmarked against three swarm intelligence algorithms and a classical multiobjective optimization method. The benchmarking process included the multiobjective evolutionary algorithm based on decomposition (MOEA/D), enhanced multiobjective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO), enhanced nondominated sorting whale optimization algorithm (NSWOA), and enhanced multiobjective grey wolf optimization algorithm (MOGWO).

The algorithms were implemented in Python 3.8 using the Pytorch framework and executed in Pycharm 2024. To ensure the integrity of the comparisons, each algorithm was executed ten times independently for each instance. The convergence and diversity of the proposed algorithms were evaluated by calculating the mean value of the results obtained across the ten runs, which was then used as the basis for the performance assessment.
Tables IV and V present the mean and standard deviation of HV and IGD values for the D3QN-NSGA-II algorithm and four comparison algorithms applied to the DHFJS problem. From these tables, it is evident that D3QN-NSGA-II achieves the highest HV values and the lowest IGD values in the majority of test cases, indicating its significant advantages in both solution convergence and diversity. For instance, in test cases such as 20J3F, 40J4F, and 150J5F, the mean HV values for D3QN-NSGA-II are 0.7851, 0.8751, and 0.8645, respectively, significantly outperforming the other algorithms. The mean IGD values are also as low as 0.2725, 0.3145, and 0.5232, showing a solution set that is much closer to the true Pareto front. To further validate the statistical significance of the improvement, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was applied to the HV metric of D3QN-NSGA-II and each of the comparison algorithms, performing pairwise significance analysis. The experimental results demonstrate that the improvements in both convergence and diversity are statistically significant, validating the effectiveness of the proposed strategy.
Fig. 5 presents the solution distribution of D3QN-NSGA-II compared to other algorithms on four test cases: 20J3F, 50J5F, 100J4F, and 150J5F. The Pareto front of D3QN-NSGA-II performs excellently in both the low $C _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and low TEC regions, with a uniformly distributed solution set that can meet the requirements of different optimization priorities. In contrast, the Pareto fronts of MOEA/D and MOPSO are more dispersed, while NSWOA and MOGWO tend to focus on optimizing a single objective in certain instances, sacrificing overall balance. The consistent performance of D3QN-NSGA-II across instances of different scales further validates its robustness and scalability, laying the foundation for deployment in complex industrial applications. Compared to the other algorithms, D3QN-NSGA-II achieves remarkable success in solving the DHFJS problem, owing to its unique design and optimization strategies. ## E. Engineering Case Study This section presents an analysis of a real production order for an engine cooling system from a domestic automotive manufacturing company, using it as an engineering case study. The theories and methods introduced in this chapter are applied to the production scheduling of this practical case. The engine factory responsible for producing this cooling system operates multiple job shops to meet order demands, and production is processed based on the order volume. This issue can be abstracted as a distributed heterogeneous job shop problem. Fig. 6 illustrates the schematic diagram of the engine cooling system. The system consists of components such as the adapter plate bracket, fan bracket, double-row deep groove ball bearings, fan hub, fan belt pulley, adapter flange, and cooling fan. The engine cooling system is produced in two job shops within the factory. Job shop 1 manufactures four parts: adapter plate bracket, fan bracket, fan hub, and adapter flange, while job shop 2 handles the production of the remaining components. Each job shop is equipped with eight machines for processing these components, including two milling machines (M1, M2), two drilling machines (M3, M4), one machining center (M5), one manual lathe (M6), and two computer numerical control lathes (M7, M8). Using the same experimental environment and algorithm parameter settings as in Part D, D3QN-NSGA-II was applied alongside methods such as MOEA/D, MOPSO, NSWOA5, and MOGWO to solve this production case. CONCLUSION The D3QN-NSGA-II algorithm incorporates the attributes of deep reinforcement learning and multiobjective optimization. By employing a dual-population strategy and a D3QN-based operator selection mechanism, the algorithm effectively balances global exploration and local exploitation, thereby enhancing both the convergence speed and the quality of solutions. A detailed description and modeling of the DHFJS problem have led to the definition of rational objective functions and constraints, thereby providing a clear framework for algorithm design and application. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms have consistently demonstrated that D3QN-NSGA-II exhibits superior performance across a range of test cases, as evidenced by metrics such as HV and IGD. These findings validate the effectiveness and superiority of D3QN-NSGA-II. From a management practice perspective, this study provides a scheduling method for the manufacturing industry that optimizes both efficiency and energy consumption. The dualpopulation evolutionary strategy guides companies in dynamically allocating search resources during production scheduling, improving global optimization capabilities. The D3QN-based operator selection mechanism helps adaptively adjust scheduling strategies based on real-time production states, enhancing the algorithm’s adaptability to complex production scenarios. The energy-saving scheduling strategy offers a feasible path to reduce machine idle energy consumption and optimize resource utilization, providing practical guidance for companies in achieving green manufacturing and cost control. Future research could explore the incorporation of additional optimization objectives (such as cost and quality) and improve the algorithms robustness against uncertainties like machine failures and demand fluctuations.

# Knowledge Transfer-Based Co-Evolutionary Search for Energy-Saving Distributed Heterogeneous Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
Tao Li , Xingchen Li , Junna Zhang , Member, IEEE, Dong Liu , and Zidong Wang , Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—This paper investigates the energy-saving distributed heterogeneous flexiblejob shop scheduling problem (ES-DHFJSP), with the dual objectives of reducing both makespan and total energy consumption. To address ES-DHFJSP, a knowledge transferbased co-evolutionary search algorithm (KTCE) is proposed. Three key components are incorporated into the algorithm. First, a greedy population initialization strategy is designed, by which the characteristics of multi-factory distributed systems are leveraged to generate superior initial individuals. Second, a dynamic neighborhood search structure centered on critical factory is developed, through which the algorithm’s capability to explore promising regions around elite solutions is enhanced. Third, a knowledge transfer mechanism centered on a factory allocation probability model is implemented, wherein the optimal factory allocations from previous generations are utilized to construct the probability model and the evolution of subsequent population is guided. The algorithm’s convergence rate is substantially improved by this mechanism. The effectiveness and efficiency of KTCE are validated through comprehensive experimental results on various benchmark instances, where superior performance is demonstrated in solving ES-DHFJSP.
Index Terms—Evolutionary algorithm, knowledge transfer, Coevolutionary search, distributed heterogeneous flexible job shop scheduling, energy-conserving.

## I. INTRODUCTION
products [1]. Traditional single-factory production systems have proven inadequate in meeting these demands, particularly in terms of rapid, large-scale production of high-quality goods [2]. Distributed manufacturing systems, characterized by multiple factories collaboratively processing product sets, have emerged as a promising solution by significantly enhancing production throughput. This approach offers notable advantages, including enhanced operational flexibility and reduced management risks [3]. Nevertheless, conventional distributed manufacturing systems continue to face critical challenges, primarily manifesting as suboptimal production efficiency and excessive energy consumption [4]. These limitations pose substantial challenges to existing job shop scheduling methodologies [5]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop advancedjob scheduling techniques that can simultaneously optimize production efficiency and minimize energy consumption.
At present, energy-saving distributed flexible job shop scheduling (ES-DFJSP) presents an effective solution to aforementioned challenges. This method requires solving three fundamental sub-problems: 1) determining optimal job-to-factory allocation schemes; 2) assigning operations to specific machines; and 3) establishing operation processing orders within each factory. The interdependence of these three subproblems makes the ES-DFJSP highly complex, characterized by a vast solution space and significant computational difficulty. Therefore, ES-DFJSP is classified as an NP-hard problem [6].
Evolutionary algorithms possess remarkable advantages in addressing multi-objective optimization challenges and have achieved notable results. Among them, noteworthy examples include the differential evolution (DE) [7], the co-evolutionary algorithm (CE) [8], [9], and the particle swarm optimization (PSO) [10], [11]. These algorithms have been extensively applied in various fields such as social networks [12], signal processing [13], computer vision [14], and the intelligent manufacturing [15], [16].
Notably, evolutionary algorithms have emerged as a viable method for addressing the ES-DFJSP problem. Although existing scheduling approaches have demonstrated promising results, they primarily focus on homogeneous factory environments. Heterogeneous distributed architectures better reflect real-world workshop production environments [17], [18]. The effect of factory heterogeneity on makespan and energy consumption has not been thoroughly investigated [19]. Furthermore, the inherent randomness in evolutionary algorithms results in substantial computational overhead when applied to high-dimensional or complex optimization problems. Consequently, efficiently addressing the ES-DHFJSP with both speed and accuracy remains a critical challenge in contemporary production scheduling research.

Breakthroughs in machine learning have driven growing interest in its synergy with evolutionary computation, fostering novel approaches to complex optimization problems [20], [21]. Knowledge transfer, which leverages insights from related source tasks to address target problems, has demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in optimization domains [22].
Evidence suggests that knowledge transfer mechanisms can effectively reduce computational overhead and enhance convergence rates of evolutionary algorithms. Motivated by these advantages, we propose integrating knowledge transfer techniques with evolutionary algorithms to solve the ES-DHFJSP.
Drawing on the aforementioned analysis, a knowledge transfer-based co-evolutionary search algorithm is proposed to solve the ES-DHFJSP. In the algorithm, the dynamic local search is integrated with global search to explore the optimal solution collaboratively, and the knowledge transfer is employed to minimize the makespan and the total energy consumption. The overall framework of the KTCE is shown in Fig. 1. The primary contributions of this paper are presented as follows:
1) A multi-factory-based greedy population initialization strategy is designed. The average processing time of jobs in each factory is adopted to generate one quarter of the initial population, which can accelerate the population convergence. Meanwhile, to ensure the diversity of the initial population, the rest of individuals are generated stochastically.
2) A dynamic neighborhood search structure centered on critical factory is presented. This structure dynamically adjusts the neighborhood search around the elite population composed of elite individuals based on the degree of global search. And the search strategy is provided by a neighborhood search strategy pool which includes three neighborhood search strategies: priority factory search strategy, equal probability factory search strategy and critical path search strategy.
3) A factory allocation-based knowledge transfer mechanism is proposed. This mechanism utilizes the factory allocation of historical elite individuals as knowledge to construct a factory allocation probability model. New knowledge is derived from the probability model and transferred to the evolving population to accelerate the acquisition of the global optimal solution.
The rest of this paper is as follows. Section II covers related work. Section III describes the problem description of ES-DHFJSP. Section IV introduces the proposed KTCE in this paper comprehensively. In Section V, relevant experiments are designed and the experimental results are analyzed and discussed. Finally, Section VI summarizes the work of this paper and analyzes future research directions.

## A. Distributed Flexible Scheduling Based on Evolutionary Algorithm

Recent research has extensively explored evolutionary approaches for distributed heterogeneous scheduling (DHS). Zhang et al. [27] introduced a biogeography-based optimization algorithm featuring local search mechanisms to address DHS with multiple process plans, employing a cosine migration rate model to escape local optima. Yang et al. [28] extracted two knowledge points from the problem structure to develop a hybrid initialization method and integrated Q-learning to dynamically adjust key parameters using population evolutionary information, resulting in accelerated the convergence. Recent studies have incorporated reinforcement learning, with Q-learning and deep-Q networks being employed for optimal operator selection [31], [32], [33].
Analysis of existing literature reveals that previous research on neighborhood search strategies development continues to exhibit several limitations. These include inadequate consideration of factory prioritization in job assignment adjustments, among others. As a result, the neighborhood search exhibits limited capacity in exploring candidate optimal solutions, which adversely affects the algorithm’s convergence properties. Thus, developing neighborhood search strategies with strong exploitation capabilities is essential to enhance the algorithm’s search performance.
Furthermore, computational resource allocation serves as another critical factor affecting algorithm performance. However, existing studies predominantly focus on selecting optimal neighborhood search strategies while largely neglecting in-depth investigation into resource allocation mechanisms. ## B. Knowledge Transfer In recent years, knowledge transfer has emerged as an effective optimization mechanism with numerous researchers exploring its integration with evolutionary algorithms. Zhang et al. [34] incorporated knowledge transfer into genetic programming, implementing task-oriented knowledge sharing within crossover operations to enhance algorithmic convergence. Lin et al. [35] developed knowledge transfer prediction and maintenance sampling techniques to mitigate negative transfer effects while improving optimization efficiency. Zheng et al. [36] integrated CE with fuzzy deep transfer learning for predicting relief demand. Furthermore, historical experience, neighborhood information, and elite individuals are frequently utilized as knowledge sources for transfer to populations, thus enhancing optimization efficiency. Jiang et al. [37] formulated a dynamic multi-objective evolutionary algorithm that utilizes historical experience to construct effective initial population pools. Wang et al. [38] introduced an EA based on decomposition with dual neighborhoods, enhancing the transfer effectiveness through acquiring knowledge from the task’s neighborhood. Guo et al. [39] developed a knowledge pool approach that preserves Paretooptimal solutions from historical environments. When encountering new environments, this approach selectively applies the most relevant knowledge to initialize populations, facilitating rapid convergence to Pareto-optimal solutions. Zhang et al. [40] implemented bidirectional knowledge transfer between dual populations (POP) and elite archives (ERT), where population diversity is maintained through inter-population individual migration while evolutionary progress is enhanced by exchanging elite solutions between populations. Peng et al. [41] proposed a micro many-objective evolutionary algorithm with knowledge transfer (μMaOEA) that enhances the performance of unoptimized niches by transferring neighborhood niches knowledge, thereby fostering the emergence of better individuals. Mitigating negative transfer remains a critical challenge in knowledge transfer optimization. Xu et al. [42] developed an adaptive EMTO framework that dynamically adjusts knowledge transfer parameters, including transfer frequency, source selection, and transfer intensity. This approach effectively maintains the equilibrium between intratask evolutionary processes and intertask knowledge transfer. Wang et al. [43] proposed a taskspecific anomaly detection framework to evaluate inter-task relationships, enabling the identification and filtering of potentially detrimental knowledge transfers. It can be seen that the combination of knowledge transfer and evolutionary algorithms can utilize the historical experience to quickly generate appropriate high-quality population when the new environment emerges. In this way, the convergence speed of the algorithm in new environments can be improved. For this reason, we consider combining knowledge transfer and evolutionary algorithms to solve ES-DHFJSP. The historical optimization experience is leveraged to guide population evolution, significantly enhancing the algorithm’s efficiency. ## III. ## IV. OUR APPROACH: KTCE This section presents an in-depth explanation of the proposed KTCE algorithm, encompassing its core methodology, the encoding and decoding mechanisms, the greedy population initialization strategy, dynamic neighborhood search structure based on critical factory, and knowledge transfer mechanism utilizing factory allocation probability models. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm’s computational complexity is provided. Output: Pareto-optimal solutions set. 1 Initialize current evaluation count NFEs = 0, elite archive A = ∅, qualification vector Qual = ∅, current iteration count t = 0, factory allocation probability model PM, and Pareto front PF₀ = ∅. 2 P₀ ← Generate initial population by greedy initialization strategy. 3 while NFES ≤ MaxNFES do 4 t = t + 1. 5 if meet the transfer condition then 6 P₀ ← Factory allocation-based knowledge transferring(PM, P₀). 7 end 8 O ← Crossover and mutation(P₀, Pc, Pm). 9 P', PF ← Obtain the new population P' and the Pareto front PF by Environmental Selection(P₀ ∪ O). 10 A ← Get the Pareto front(A ∪ PF). 11 Qual ← Update qualification vector. 12 PM ← Factory Allocation-based knowledge learning(PF/PF₀, PM, σ). 13 PF', P'' ← Dynamic neighborhood search based on critical factory(A, ε, Qual, P', NFEs, MaxNFEs, σ). 14 A ← PF', P₀ ← P'', PF₀ ← PF'. 15 end ``` ## A. The Main Idea of KTCE The KTCE algorithm operates through the following key phases. Initially, a multi-factory-based greedy population initialization strategy is employed to generate superior initial individuals. Subsequently, a factory allocation-based knowledge transfer mechanism guides population optimization. The algorithm then executes global search across the entire population, while implementing neighborhood search within an elite population A comprising superior individuals. Finally, a dynamic neighborhood search structure centered on critical factory is utilized, which evaluates the current Pareto front using qualification vector Qual and conducts adaptive neighborhood exploration. This framework enables thorough investigation of promising solution regions. The collaboration between dual populations enhances the algorithm’s capability to identify optimal solutions. The complete algorithmic procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1. ## B. Encoding and Decoding Schema 1) Encoding Schema: This paper employs a three-layer vector $s = [ O S , M S , F A ]$ as the encoding schema. OS determines the processing order, and its length is equivalent to operations count SH, where $\begin{array} { r } { S H = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } { \overline { { n _ { i } } } } } \end{array}$ . Job numbers are assigned to elements, with each number pointing to a specific job operation. MS represents the machine selection for each operation, and its length is equal to OS. The k-th element indicates the machine number for processing the corresponding operation. FA prescribes the processing factory for each job, and its length is $N .$ The i-th element denotes the factory number assigned to the i-th job. 2) Decoding Schema: Firstly, the jobs are assigned to the corresponding factory according to the FA. And then the processing machine is selected for each job by the MS vector. Finally, the operation sequence on each machine is determined based on OS to form a complete scheduling scheme. Fig. 3 shows the scheduling scheme obtained after decoding. ## C. Multi-Factory-Based Greedy Population Initialization Strategy In evolutionary computation, the quality and uniformity of the initial population significantly influence the efficiency of solution space exploration and algorithmic convergence rate [45]. Hence, the development of effective population initialization strategies is crucial for solving optimization problems. This paper proposes a multi-factory-based greedy population initialization strategy that constructs superior initial population while preserving the diversity. First, the average total processing time $A T _ { i , f }$ of any job across all factories is computed by: $$ A T _ {i, f} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n _ {i}} \frac {\sum_ {m \in M _ {i , j , f}} T _ {i , j , f , m}}{M _ {i , j , f} ^ {n}}\tag{11} $$ The factories are arranged in ascending order according to $A T _ { i , f }$ . Subsequently, i-th job is assigned to the factory with the minimum $A T _ { i , f }$ . This process repeats until all jobs are assigned. This greedy initialization approach facilitates the generation of high-quality FA chromosomes while enhancing algorithm convergence. For example, given the current factory set $F =$ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, average total processing times for job $I _ { i }$ at each factory are calculated as $A T = \{ 1 9 . 6 , 1 7 . 0 , 3 1 . 2 , 2 4 . 2 , 2 1 . 4 \}$ Therefore, factory $F _ { 2 }$ achieves the minimum average total processing time. Under the greedy strategy, $I _ { i }$ is allocated to $F _ { 2 }$ Alternatively, the randomized strategy assigns $I _ { i }$ to any factory in F with equal probability. However, excessive use of greedy strategies may lead to limited search range of the initial population, resulting in falling into local optima. FA vectors of one quarter of the initial population are generated by the proposed greedy strategy, while the remaining are generated by the random strategy. Following population initialization, a global search with extended step size is implemented to expand the exploration space and identify promising solution regions. The algorithm employs two crossover operators [46]: Priority Operation Crossover (POX) for operation sequence crossover, and Universal Crossover (UX) for machine selection and factory allocation crossover. Subsequently, two mutation strategies are applied according to probability $P m \colon 1 )$ position exchange between two randomly selected operations in the operation sequence; and 2) reassignment of processing machines for randomly selected operations to alternative available machines. Environmental selection is performed using non-dominated sorting [47].

## D. Dynamic Neighborhood Search Structure Centered on Critical Factory While global search with large step sizes effectively expands the solution space, identifying optimal solutions within extensive search domains under time constraints remains challenging, particularly when exploring regions around specific solution targets. Neighborhood search methods have emerged as an effective approach and have been extensively investigated [48], [49], [50]. Consequently, neighborhood search techniques are essential for conducting intensive exploration around elite solutions. The synergistic integration of global and neighborhood search mechanisms substantially enhances the algorithm’s capability to identify optimal solutions. In the context of ES-DHFJSP optimization, critical factory and critical path factors play vital roles. Their definitions are as follows: \- The critical factory is defined as the factory with the maximum completion time. \- The critical path refers to the sequence of operations requiring the longest total processing time from start to end. Accordingly, three neighborhood search strategies combined with a dynamic search structure are developed to maintain an equilibrium between neighborhood and global search operations. These local search strategies are detailed as follows: 1) LS1(Neighborhood Search Strategy Based on Priority Factory): The neighborhood strategy focuses on the adjustment of factory assignment for the critical factory. Firstly, calculate the finish time of factories other than the critical one and rank them in ascending sequence, where the higher the ranking of the factory, the smaller the makespan, and the higher the priority. Then select a job at random from the critical factory and add it to the factory with the highest priority. 2) LS (Neighborhood Search Strategy Based on Equal Probability Factory): This neighborhood strategy also focuses on the adjustment of the critical factory. It concentrates on slightly increasing the search space to explore solutions more effectively in the neighborhood. $L S _ { 2 }$ is to select a factory with moderate probability from other factories except for the critical factory. Then, a job is randomly extracted from the critical factory and added to the chosen factory. 3) LS3(Neighborhood Search Strategy Based on Critical Path): This neighborhood strategy focuses on the adjustment of the critical path, which exchanges the positions of two operations randomly. It should be emphasized that excessive allocation of computational resources to neighborhood search may result in premature convergence to local optima. Therefore, efficient resource allocation between neighborhood and global search operations is crucial for enhancing algorithmic performance [51], [52]. This paper introduces a dynamic neighborhood search framework that adaptively distributes computational resources based on search requirements at different optimization stages. First, two variables are defined as: (1) LST represents the frequency of neighborhood searches; (2) maxLST denotes the current maximum allowable number of neighborhood searches, calculated as follows: $$ m a x L S T = \left\lceil \varepsilon \times \frac {N F E s}{M a x N F E s} \right\rceil\tag{12} $$ During the initial phase of KTCE, computational resources are predominantly allocated to global search for broad exploration. As the algorithm progresses through iterations, the effectiveness of large-scale exploration diminishes, necessitating the allocation of computational resources to neighborhood search around elite solutions for identifying promising optimal candidates. Additionally, a qualification vector Qual is introduced to filter individuals eligible for neighborhood search. It has the same size as ${ \mathcal { A } } ,$ and both are initially empty. Upon adding a new solution $p _ { i }$ to $\mathcal { A } , Q u a l _ { p _ { i } }$ is added to Qual and initialized to 1. Correspondingly, when $p _ { i }$ is removed from $\mathcal { A } , Q u a l _ { p _ { i } }$ is removed. For solution $p _ { i }$ in ${ \mathcal { A } } .$ , neighborhood search is activated only when $Q u a l _ { p _ { i } } = 1$ Specifically, $p _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ is defined as the obtained individual through neighborhood search. $e n d _ { f }$ denotes the termination indicator and $e n d \mathrm { { \_ } n a x }$ represents the maximum threshold value of endf, calculated as follows: $$ e n d _ {\max} = \left\lceil m a x L S T \times \frac {2}{3} \right\rceil\tag{13} $$ When $e n d _ { f } > e n d _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ , indicating that $e n d _ { f }$ has exceeded its upper bound, the neighborhood search performed on solution $p _ { i }$ fails to yield a better solution. Then, $Q u a l _ { p _ { i } } = Q u a l _ { p _ { i } } - 1$ Simultaneously, $p _ { i }$ is excluded from subsequent neighborhood search iterations. This mechanism significantly reduces redundant exploitation. Algorithm 2 presents the pseudo-code of the dynamic neigh borhood search structure based on critical factory. ## E. Factory Allocation-Based Knowledge Transfer Mechanism Beyond determining operation sequences and machine assignments, ES-DHFJSP necessitates factory allocation decisions, substantially expanding the problem dimensionality. Consequently, we partition the solution space into multiple subspaces based on factory allocation patterns, with each subspace representing a distinct allocation strategy. Upon identifying elite solutions, selected individuals are directed to explore promising regions within these elite solution subspaces. To facilitate this approach, we develop a knowledge transfer mechanism utilizing a factory allocation probability model. This framework leverages historical elite solutions’ factory assignments as transferable knowledge to guide the current population toward promising subspaces. This mechanism enhances both population convergence rate and solution quality. To ensure effective subspace exploration, knowledge transfer is implemented at regular $T \cdot$ -generation intervals, where ${ p s / 1 0 }$ individuals are selected for factory allocation adjustment using the probability model, thereby concentrating the search within elite solution subspaces. The detailed implementation of this factory allocation-based knowledge transfer mechanism proceeds as follows:

Initially, all factories share a uniform probability distribution. Specifically, for any job $I _ { i }$ $\begin{array} { r } { P M _ { i } = \left\lceil 0 , \frac { 1 } { n _ { f } } , \frac { 2 } { n _ { f } } , \dots , 1 \right\rceil } \end{array}$ Assume the elite population is denoted as $\bar { P } { F _ { t } }$ after the completion of the t-th iteration. Then, a new Pareto front $P F _ { t + 1 } ^ { 1 }$ is generated after the $( t + 1 )$ -th global search, and the newly added elite individuals are collected to form the set $D i f _ { t + 1 }$ , it is shown as: $$ D i f _ {t + 1} = P F _ {t + 1} ^ {1} / P F _ {t}\tag{14} $$ Then, the FA encoding of each elite individual $d _ { i } \in D i f _ { t + 1 }$ is obtained, and it is denoted as $d F A _ { i } .$ Afterwards update the factory allocation probability model PM based on $d F A _ { i }$ . The update formula is shown as: $$ P M _ {j, f} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} P M _ {j, f} + \sigma \times (n _ {f} - f - 1) & \text { if } f \geq d F A _ {i, j} \\ P M _ {j, f} - \sigma \times (f + 1), & \text { otherwise } \end{array} \right.\tag{15} $$ where σ represents the learning intensity, j is the job index, and $d F A _ { i , j }$ denotes the FA encoding of the j-th job in individual $d F A _ { i } .$ In Algorithm 3, the pseudo-code for factory allocationbased knowledge learning is outlined. 2) Factory Allocation-based Knowledge Transferring: First, the vector $Q = [ P _ { 1 } , P _ { 2 } , \dots , P _ { r } ]$ is obtained based on the nondominated sorting of the population, where $P _ { i }$ represents the vector of individuals with Pareto rank $i ,$ and the highest rank is denoted as $r .$ Then, select individuals of this rank as transfer individuals starting from $P _ { r }$ . If the number of individuals is insufficient, the individuals from the previous rank are selected until the number of extracted individuals reaches ${ p s / 1 0 }$ . The factory assignments of each transfer individual are adjusted according to the PM. The pseudo-code of factory allocation-based knowledge transferring is shown in Algorithm 4. Time Complexity of KTCE The KTCE algorithm comprises the following three components: evolutionary process, neighborhood search and knowledge transfer. The complexity of each component is described as follows: 1) Evolutionary Process: Within the global search, the complexity are decomposed into two distinct phases: $O ( p s )$ for the crossover-mutation phase and $O ( p s ^ { 2 } )$ for the environmental selection phase. Therefore, the evolutionary process requires $O ( p s ^ { 2 } )$ 2) Neighborhood Search: The neighborhood search section has a time complexity of $O ( s i z e ( A ) * ( m a x L S T + N ) )$ The learning section requires $O ( s i z e ( \mathcal { A } ) * N )$ . Hence, the total complexity of the neighborhood search section is $O ( s i z e ( A ) * ( m a x L S T + N ) )$ 3) Knowledge Transfer: The time complexity of knowledge transfer stage is $O ( ( p s + r ) * p s )$ We define Iter as iteration count. Hence, the aggregate complexity of the KTCE is $O ( p s ^ { 2 } * I t e r )$ .

## V. EXPERIMENT RESULTS AND ANALYSIS The current section conducts a in-depth experimental evaluation of the KTCE algorithm. The experimental analysis is structured into five subsections: first, CPLEX is employed to verify the ES-DHFJSP model; second, the benchmark instances and performance metrics are introduced; third, parameter calibration procedures are detailed; furthermore, to execute individual component, ablation experiments are carried out; finally, comparative analyses against state-of-the-art multi-objective optimal algorithms are performed. KTCE is programmed using Python 3.9. All algorithms run on an Intel(R) Core (TM) i5-10210 U CPU @ 1.60 GHz 2.11 GHz and 8 GB of RAM. ## A. Model Verification To verify the correctness of the ES-DHFJSP model, CPLEX 22.1.0 (full version) is employed. The model is coded in the native optimization language of CPLEX and verified on six generated small-scale instances. Each instance contains 4-6jobs, each having 5 operations, along with 2 or 3 factories, each equipped with 5 machines. The maximum runtimes of CPLEX and KTCE is limited to 600 seconds. Utilizing the optimal solution obtained by CPLEX as the benchmark, the time for KTCE to reach the benchmark is recorded. To minimize variability, we executed 10 independent runs on each instance for both CPLEX and KTCE. The average computation times are computed as the final times. The computational results are presented in Table II. The results verify the correction of the model. Furthermore, they demonstrate that KTCE converges to the optimal solution within a desirable time.

## B. Instances and Metrics The evaluation of KTCE is conducted on 20 instances of varying scales. The job count N takes values from {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100, 150, 200}, while the factory count $n _ { f }$ spans the interval [2, 7]. All factories contain $m = 5$ machines. In addition, any machine consumes 4kWh for processing and 1kWh for idle states. The instances are available at https: //wewnyin.github.io/wenyingong/Software/DQCE-code.zip. Two standard performance metrics are employed to evaluate the multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs): hypervolume (HV) and inverted generational distance (IGD). The HV metric quantifies the algorithm’s comprehensive performance by computing the hypervolume bounded by the Pareto front and a reference point, where elevated HV indicates superior overall performance. The IGD metric characterizes comprehensive performance through the distance separating the true and approximated Pareto fronts, with smaller IGD values suggesting better convergence and solution diversity.

Ablation Experiment To assess individual algorithmic component’s contribution, three variant algorithms are constructed: 1) KTCE1, which excludes the greedy population initialization strategy; 2) KTCE2, which omits the dynamic neighborhood search structure; and 3) KTCE3, which eliminates the knowledge transfer mechanism. data.content:
## VI. CONCLUSION
This paper develops a knowledge transfer-based coevolutionary search algorithm for ES-DHFJSP. The algorithm has incorporated three key components: First, a greedy population initialization strategy is developed. FA vectors of one quarter of the initial population are generated based on average processing times, while the remaining individuals’ FA vectors are generated stochastically. Implementation of this methodology elevates genotypic quality within the population and significantly enhances convergence rate. Second, a dynamic framework that has combined three critical factory-based neighborhood search strategies, enabling effective exploration of promising solutions while maintaining global search capabilities. Third, a knowledge transfer mechanism that has utilized factory allocation probability models to preserve high-quality factory assignment patterns and accelerate algorithmic convergence. Comprehensive experimental results across 20 benchmark instances have demonstrated that KTCE has outperformed existing algorithms in addressing ES-DHFJSP.
Although the proposed KTCE exhibits excellent performance in ES-DHFJSP, it still has some deficiency that need to be solved in future work. Such as, in the later stage of iteration, the negative transfer may increase significantly and lead to falling into local optima. Additionally, the factors considered in the update of the probability model are also relatively limited. Therefore, investigating more efficient model to solve ES-DHFJSP problems is a future research direction.

# An efficient memetic algorithm for distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers
<drawing id="im-e5d47f23ff2115fdf069ba128946a7e2-0001" format="jpg" path="An efficient memetic algorithm for distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers-316215e1.blocks.assets/8deb6a13445022441e075d9603c02f53acf1c70af875bed0eec8862c9ca13ef4.jpg" src="" />
Qiang Luo, Qianwang Deng ⇑, Guiliang Gong, Like Zhang, Wenwu Han, Kexin Li
State Key Laboratory of Advanced Design and Manufacturing for Vehicle Body, Hunan University, Changsha 410082, China

## a r t i c l e i n f o
Article history: Received 3 September 2019 Revised 30 June 2020 Accepted 3 July 2020 Available online 19 July 2020
Keywords: Distributed flexible job shop scheduling Operation transfer Memetic algorithm Multi-objective optimization Taguchi method

## a b s t r a c t
The traditional distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP) assumes that operations of a job cannot be transferred between different factories. However, in real-world production settings, the operations of a job may need to be processed in different factories owing to requirements of economic globalization or complexity of the job. Hence, in this paper, we propose a distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers (DFJSPT), in which operations of a job can be processed in different factories. An efficient memetic algorithm (EMA) is proposed to solve the DFJSPT with the objectives of minimizing the makespan, maximum workload, and total energy consumption of factories. In the proposed EMA, a well-designed chromosome presentation and initialization methods are presented to obtain a high-quality initial population. Several crossover and mutation operators and three effective neighborhood structures are designed to expand the search space and accelerate the convergence speed of the solution. Forty benchmark instances of the DFJSPT are constructed to evaluate the EMA and facilitate further studies. The Taguchi method of design of experiments is used to obtain the best combination of key EMA parameters. Extensive computational experiments are carried out to compare the EMA with three well-known algorithms from the literature. The computational results show that the EMA can obtain better solutions for approximately 90% of the tested benchmark instances compared to the three well known algorithms, thereby demonstrating the DFJSPT’s competitive performance and efficiency.

## 1. Introduction
Flexible job shop scheduling (FJSP) has been widely studied in recent decades (Burdett, Corry, Yarlagadda, Eustace, & Smith, 2019; Burdett & Kozan, 2018; Deliktas, Torkul, & Ustun, 2019; Deng, et al., 2017; Gong, Chiong, Deng, & Gong, 2019). In FJSP, all jobs are assumed to be processed in only one location (Al Aqel, Li, & Gao, 2019; Deng, et al., 2017; Wang, Jiang, Wang, Zhang, & Wang, 2018). However, in real-world manufacturing, products are normally processed in different factories, which are often distributed in different regions because cooperative production with different factories has obvious advantages in terms of response speed and production cost (Imen Chaouch, Driss, & Ghedira, 2019; Pan, Gao, Wang, Liang, & Li, 2019; Ying & Lin, 2018). Therefore, the distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP), in which jobs can be processed in different factories, has attracted increasingly more attention of researchers in the past decade (Chang & Liu, 2017; Iman Chaouch, Driss, & Ghedira, 2017).
The DFJSP addresses production scheduling problems existing in distributed manufacturing environments, wherein jobs are processed collaboratively by a number of flexible manufacturing units (FMUs) (De Giovanni & Pezzella, 2010; Jeong & Yim, 2009). An FMU consists of a number of enterprises (or production units); each enterprise includes several machines with different process quantities or performances (Liu, Chen, & Chou, 2014). The DFJSP is required to arrange the jobs to be processed in these enterprises, meeting objectives, such as minimizing the makespan, total machine workload, and total energy consumption. (Li, Duan, Cao, Lin, & Han, 2018; Marzouki, Driss, & Ghedira, 2018). The DFJSP has three sub-problems, which are as follows: (1) factory assignment, i.e., selecting a factory for each operation; (2) machine assignment, i.e., selecting a machine to process each operation; and (3) operation sequencing, i.e., sequencing the operations, obeying the constraints of factories, machines, and job processes simultaneously.
To date, only a limited number of researchers have studied the DFJSP. For example, Giovanni and Pezzella proposed an improved genetic algorithm (GA) to solve the DFJSP, in which an ingenious chromosome encoding and a local search strategy were integrated (De Giovanni & Pezzella, 2010). Chang and Liu presented a hybrid GA for the DFJSP with a novel encoding mechanism, and a few effective crossover and mutation operators (Chang & Liu, 2017). Liu, Chen, and Chou proposed an improved GA to solve the DFJSP, in which a refined encoding operator was designed to guarantee the diversity of chromosomes (Liu, et al., 2014). Marzouki, Driss and Ghedira proposed a chemical reaction meta-heuristic optimization method to solve the DFJSP with the objective of minimizing the makespan (Marzouki, et al., 2018). Based on a constructive procedure, Ziaee developed a fast heuristic algorithm to solve the DFJSP very quickly (Ziaee, 2013). Lu et al. developed an improved GA for the DFJSP, in which a novel concise chromosome representation was designed (Lu, Wu, Tan, Peng, & Chen, 2015). Li et al. constructed a hybrid Pareto-based tabu search algorithm to handle the DFJSP with the objectives of minimizing the makespan, maximum workload, total workload, and earliness/tardiness (Li, et al., 2018).

From the above, we can make the following observations: all the studies on the DFJSPs assumed that the jobs could not be transferred among different factories, i.e., operations of a job must be processed in the same factory; however, in real-world production systems, certain jobs may have to be processed in different factories because of reasons, such as complexity of operations or economic globalization. In addition, under energy-saving era, most of researchers focused on single objective (makespan) in DFJSP, which led to the production managers focused on economic indicator but ignored other important factors, such as energy consumption generated by processing and transferring jobs.
Inspired by these findings, in this study, we propose a distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers (DFJSPT), in which the jobs can be transferred among factories. The memetic algorithms (MAs), which hybridize evolutionary algorithms with local search (Burdett & Kozan, 2014; Chiong, Weise, & Michalewicz, 2012; Gong, et al., 2019; Kannan & Ramaraj, 2010), have delivered promising performance for solving multi-objective FJSPs (Frutos, Olivera, & Tohmé, 2010; Gong, Deng, Gong, Liu, & Ren, 2018; Wenchao, Xinyu, & Baolin, 2016; Yuan & Xu, 2013; Yuan & Xu, 2015). Motivated by their work and based on the fact that it’s hard or even impossible to obtain the optimal solutions in the acceptable time for the NP-hard problems (eg., FJSP (Gong, et al., 2020), DFJSP (De Giovanni & Pezzella, 2010), and our DFJSPT) by using mixed integer programming approaches, we present an effective memetic algorithm (EMA) to solve our proposed DFJSPT with the objectives of minimizing the makespan, maximum workload of factories, and total energy consumption. In the EMA, an effective initialization method that combines global, local, and random selections, and a crossover operator are used to obtain a highquality initial population and improve the solution diversity. In addition, a well-designed local search operator (LSO) is proposed and integrated into the EMA to improve its convergence speed and fully exploit its solution space. In addition, 40 benchmark instances are constructed to test the EMA’s performance and facilitate our future study. Finally, a suitable combination of key parameters in the EMA, which includes population size (POP\_size), crossover rate (CR\_rate), mutation rate (MU\_rate), and local search rate (LS\_rate) is obtained by using the Taguchi method of Design of Experiments (DOE) (Montgomery, 2008). Extensive experiments carried out on these 40 instances confirm the superior performance of the EMA compared to the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) (Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, & Meyarivan, 2002), non-dominated neighbor immune algorithm (NNIA) (Gong, Jiao, Du, & Bo, 2008) and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm III (NSGA-III) (Deb & Jain, 2014).
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, a mathematical model of the DFJSPT is presented. In Section 3, the EMA is described in detail. The numerical experiments and discussions are presented in Section 4. Finally, we draw some conclusions and describe the future work in Section 5.

Problem description and mathematical mode The DFJSPT consists of J jobs assignments $\left\{ J _ { 1 } , J _ { 2 } , \ldots , J _ { I } \right\}$ , which need to be processed in F factories $\{ F _ { 1 } , F _ { 2 } , \dots , F _ { F } \}$ , and these factories are geographically distributed in several regions. The processing time and unit energy consumption of each machine for operation $O _ { j o }$ are ascertained in advance. Three objectives, including makespan, maximum workload of factories, and total energy consumption, are considered in this model. The assumptions made in this model are as follows: No suspension or interruption is allowed once the processing of an operation is started. Each machine can only process one operation at a time. The non-dominated sorting operator is used to evaluate the quality of individuals by distinguishing the dominant relationship between individuals, and the crowding distance is used to enhance the diversity of the solutions and to obtain a uniform non-dominated solution set. The main steps of NSGA-II are described as follows. Firstly, the parent and offspring population of generation t with the same size N, i.e., $P _ { t }$ and C, respectively are defined. Next, a new population $R _ { t }$ is obtained by combining P and $C _ { t } , \mathrm { i . e . , } R _ { t } = P _ { t } \cup C _ { t }$ . It should be noted that another operator ‘‘crowding distance computing” is used as a reference to select the individuals when the same rank appears in $R _ { t } ,$ and an individual with a larger crowding distance will be assigned to $P _ { t + 1 }$ . ## 3.2.1. Framework of EMA
The main steps of EMA are as follows:
Step 1: setting the key parameters.
Step 2: performing encoding and decoding of the chromosome.
Step 3: initialization. Set U = 0 and initialize the population P(U) with N individuals.
Step 4: offspring generation. Generate the population P’(U) (size of N ) and P‘‘(U) (size of N ) by using crossover and mutation operators, respectively, based on P(U).
Step 5: population combination. Combine P(U), P’(U), and P‘‘(U) to generate population R(U); the non-dominated sorting and crowding distance computing operators are applied for R(U).
Step 6: local search. According to the sorting results, select the top 15% individuals of R(U) to execute the LSO; a new population R’(U) (of same size as R(U)) is obtained after performing the LSO

Step 7: elite selection and reservation. Perform non-dominated sorting and crowding distance operators for R’(U) to get the population R’’(U); select the best N individuals of R’’(U) to generate P (U + 1).
Step 8: stop criteria. If the stop criteria are satisfied, output P(U); otherwise, go back to step 4.

Based on the proposed three-layer encoding method, an initialization method called GLR, which includes global, local, and random selection methods (Yang, Zhang, Liang, & Yuan, 2009), is designed to generate the initial population. According to (Zhang, Gao, & Shi, 2011), 60%, 30%, and 10% proportions of global, local, and random selections have been proved to be effective for solving the FJSP. Therefore, we adopt the aforementioned proportions of these three selection methods in the EMA. The pseudo code of GLR is given in Algorithm 1, and the results related to the testing

## 3.2.4. Crossover operator
In the crossover operator, only a multiple operation crossover (MOX) for the OS vector is designed, because not all of the machines can handle every operation. The aim of MOX is to increase the population diversity by a crossover on an operation sequence. The key steps of MOX are described below, in which $P _ { 1 }$ and $P _ { 2 }$ are defined as two parents, and $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ are the offspring. Assume that $P _ { 1 }$ and $P _ { 2 }$ have been produced and are as shown in Fig. 4. The offspring $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ are generated from the following steps:
Step 1: randomly generate two positions on the OS vector, marked Position 1 and Position 2. As shown in Fig. 4, Positions 1 and 2 are 4 and 9, respectively.
Step 2: find the gene fragments between Positions 1 and 2 in $P _ { 1 } ,$ which is [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2]; find the gene fragment between Positions 1 and 2 in $P _ { 2 } ,$ which is [2, 1, 4, 3, 4, 3]. Note that the operations in the two gene fragments are determined again according to the chromosome encoding, for example, [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] corresponds to $[ O _ { 3 1 } , O _ { 2 1 } , O _ { 1 1 } , O _ { 1 2 } , O _ { 1 3 } , O _ { 2 2 } ] .$
Step 3: find all the positions in $P _ { 2 }$ with the same information as [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] from the left to the right; the positions found in $P _ { 2 }$ are the first, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth.
Step 4: insert the genes of [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] in $P _ { 1 }$ to the first, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth positions of $C _ { 1 }$ from the left to the right; insert the genes of $P _ { 2 } ,$ except those in the first, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth positions, into $C _ { 1 }$ from the left to the right.

## 3.2.5. Mutation operator A population generated by the GLR method may be a partial optimal solution, because the machines with the longest processing time may be assigned to some operations during the process of balancing the makespan and workload of the factories. To avoid this problem, we propose an ‘‘inversing sequencing mutation” (ISM) of three successive genes on the OS vector, and a ‘‘replacing machine mutation” (RMM) of the two positions on the MA vector. The ISM reduces the three objectives by optimizing the sequence of operations, while the RMM reduces the processing time and transfer time by changing the processing machines of the two operations. At every iteration, only either the ISM or RMM is used, i.e., if a random number from 0 to 1 is greater than 0.5, the RMM is used, and ISM is used, otherwise. To make the ISM and RMM clearer, assume that a parent individual $\mathsf { P } _ { 3 }$ has been generated. Now, the offspring C3 by the ISM and C4 by the RMM are generated from the following steps. Firstly, offspring ${ \sf C } _ { 3 }$ is acquired by following steps: Step 1: randomly generate two positions on the OS vector in $\mathrm { P } _ { 3 } ,$ marked Position 1 and Position 2. As shown in Fig. 5, Positions 1 and 2 are 3 and 5, respectively. Step 2: inverse the genes [4, 3, 2] between Positions 1 and 2 on the OS vector and keep the other genes unchangeable. This leads to a new offspring ${ \sf C } _ { 3 }$ being acquired. Next, offspring $\mathsf { C } _ { 4 }$ is obtained by following steps: Step 1: randomly generate two positions on the MA vector in $\mathrm { P } _ { 3 } ,$ marked Position 3 and Position 4. As shown in Fig. 6, Positions 3 and 4 are 3 and 10, respectively. Step 2: specify the operations in Positions 3 and $^ { 4 , }$ which are $O _ { 1 3 }$ and $O _ { 4 1 }$ respectively. List the alternative machines (excluding the current machines) for $O _ { 1 3 }$ and $O _ { 4 1 }$ . The machines with the shortest processing times, i.e., $M _ { 3 }$ and $M _ { 1 }$ are selected to replace the original machines $M _ { 4 }$ in Position 3 and $M _ { 5 }$ in Position 4, respectively. Step 3: update the factory arrangements from $\left[ F _ { 2 } , F _ { 2 } \right]$ to $\left[ F _ { 1 } , F _ { 1 } \right]$ in Positions 3 and $^ { 4 , }$ and keep the other genes unchanged. Thus, a new offspring $\mathsf { C } _ { 4 }$ can be obtained. ## 3.2.6. Local search operator (LSO) In this section, an LSO is proposed to accelerate the convergence speed and expand the solution space of the EMA. Many previous studies, such as Yuan and Xu (2015) and Wang, Zhou, Xu, Wang, and Liu (2012), demonstrated that the makespan for a predetermined scheduling could be minimized only by moving the operations on the critical path (also called the critical operations path). Hence, taking inspiration from the aforementioned studies, here, we design three methods for the LSO. The first method swaps two positions of the critical operations (LSO\_SP) based on critical blocks (Li, Pan, & Liang, 2010). The second method converts the current factory and machine to other alternatives with a minimum processing time (LSO\_MPT). The third method replaces the current factory and machine with other alternatives that can reduce the transfer time to the maximum extent possible (LSO\_RTT). The core pseudo code of the LSO is shown in Algorithm 2, while two other pseudo codes related to the three LSOs are given in Algorithms 3 and 4 respectively.

## 4. Numerical experiments and discussions
The proposed EMA for the DFJSPT was executed in MATLAB R2016 and computed on a PC equipped with an Intel<sup></sup> Core i5 3.3 GHz and 8 GB RAM processor. To eliminate extraneous solutions during the computations, 10 numerical experiments were conducted for each benchmark instance.

## 4.1. Construction of the DFJSPT benchmarks
To test the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed EMA, we built new benchmarks named DFMs 01–40 by extending the current popular benchmarks from the FJSP (Hurink, Jurisch, & Thole, 1994). To compare the performance of the EMA with the other previous effective multi-objective algorithms for solving the DFJSPT, DFMs 01–40 were classified as small size instances (DFMs 01– 15), middle size instances (DFMs 16–30), and large size instances (DFMs 31–40). The three types of instances were generated by setting the available factory collection, maximum machine rank, and available machine numbers in each factory as [2, 4, 6], [6, 8, 10], and [1–2, 1–3, 1–4] respectively. In addition, the transfer times of jobs were predetermined as 30 units for a job transfer between machines in the same factory and 60 units for a job transfer between different factories). The energy consumption for each job during the transfer was taken as 6 units. The instance information used in this study can be downloaded on line at https:/ github.com/hnulq191817880/mygit2019.git.
Q. Luo et al. / Expert Systems with Applications 160 (2020) 113721

## 4.2. Performance metrics
To evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm, two outstanding metrics, namely the C-metric (Wisittipanich & Kachitvichyanukul, 2013) and the inverted generational distance (IGD) (Yuan & Xu, 2015) were adopted. These two metrics have been widely used in multi-objective optimization (Gong, et al., 2020; Gong, Deng, Chiong, Gong, & Huang, 2019; Gong, Deng, Gong, Liu, & Ren, 2018; Gong, et al., 2018). The detailed computation of these metrics is explained as follows.
(1) The C-metric is computed using the following equation:
<equation id="eq-e5d47f23ff2115fdf069ba128946a7e2-0013" format="latex">$$
C (A, B) = \frac {\left| \{\mathbf {b} \in B | \exists \mathbf {a} \in A : \mathbf {a} \succ \mathbf {b} \} \right|}{\mid B \mid}\tag{12}
$$</equation>
where the sets A and B represent the solutions in the first Pareto front of two algorithms, and the $C \left( A , B \right)$ means the proportion of solutions in set A that dominates the solutions in set B. The | B | represents the number of solutions in B. C (A, B) = 0 indicates that there are no solutions in A that dominate any solution in B, while $C \left( A , \right.$ B) = 1 denotes that there is at least one solution in A, which dominates all the solutions in B. The bigger the percentage of C (A, B), the better the solution set A.
(2) The IGD of set A can be calculated using the following equation:
<equation id="eq-e5d47f23ff2115fdf069ba128946a7e2-0014" format="latex">$$
I G D (A, P ^ {*}) = \frac {1}{| P ^ {*} |} \sum_ {x \in P ^ {*}} \min _ {y \in A} d (x, y)\tag{13}
$$</equation>
where $P ^ { * }$ indicates the set of non-dominated solutions of the first Pareto front; |P\*| indicates the size of $P ^ { * } ;$ and d $( x , y )$ is equal to the Euclidean distance between points x and y. Note that the smaller the percentage of IGD (A, P\*), the better the performance of A. In this study, $P ^ { * }$ was derived from the non-dominated solutions of 10 runs for each instance, using the EMA, NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III. Additionally, the objectives of the non-dominated solutions in A and $P ^ { * }$ were normalized as shown below.
<equation id="eq-e5d47f23ff2115fdf069ba128946a7e2-0015" format="latex">$$
\tilde {f} \mathrm{i} (x) = \frac {f _ {i} (x) - f _ {i} ^ {\min}}{f _ {i} ^ {\max} - f _ {i} ^ {\min}}, i = 1, 2, 3\tag{14}
$$</equation>
where $f _ { i } ^ { m i n }$ and $f _ { i } ^ { m a x }$ are the minimal and maximal values of the ith objective among all the solutions.

## 4.3. Parameter setting
The parameters in EMA mainly include the size of population (POP\_size), probability of crossover (CR\_rate), probability of mutation $( M U _ { - } r a t e ) ,$ , and rate of local search (LS\_rate). Compared to the other methods of determining the key parameters, the Taguchi method yields a superior performance and has been widely used (Lin, Gow, & Tsai, 2011; Zheng & Wang, 2015). Referring to the parameter setting in Kackar (1985), an orthogonal experiment based on the Taguchi method was designed to obtain the best combination of the parameters. In this study, four levels for each parameter (POP\_size: [50, 100, 150, 200], CR\_rate: [0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9], MU\_rate: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], and LS\_rate: [0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2]) were selected, and 16 combinations were formed under the Taguchi method as shown in Table 3. To evaluate the three objectives accurately, a normalization value named the objectives deviation sum (ODS) was computed using Equation (15) as shown below.
<equation id="eq-e5d47f23ff2115fdf069ba128946a7e2-0016" format="latex">$$
O D S (n) = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {3} \left(\frac {X _ {m n} - \min \{X _ {m} \}}{\min \{X _ {m} \}} * 1 0 0\right) \quad n = 1, 2, \dots , 1 6\tag{15}
$$</equation>
where $X _ { m n }$ denotes the average value of the objective m for the nth combination of parameters; and $\{ X _ { m } \}$ indicates the average number set of objective m for each combination. The smaller the ODS, the better the objectives are met.
Fig. 8 shows the results for the average ODS for each parameter level corresponding to Table 3. To quantify the results, the average ODS was calculated using four tests with the same layer. According to the result presented in Fig. 8, the final determined combination of parameters in this study was POP\_size = 150, CR\_rate = 0.7, MU\_rate = 0.4, and LS\_rate = 0.15.

## 4.6. Comparison with other algorithms To further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed EMA, we compared the same with the NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III using three experiments. The reasons for choosing those algorithms to make a comparison with EMA are as follows: (i) they have been widely used to solve multi-objective optimization problems; (ii) they use the non-dominated sorting method to deal with multiobjectives; and (iii) they are usually used as classical algorithms to evaluate the effectiveness of new algorithms with multiobjective problems (Siqueira, Freitas Souza, & Souza, 2020; Liang, et al., 2015; Ticona Gutierrez, Adamatti, & Bravo, 2019; Zhu, et al., 2019). The complete comparison experiment was carried out in two stages. In the first stage, we wanted to find the runtime of the algorithms under the iteration stop criterion. To avoid unfeasible solutions during the evolutionary processing, the crossover, mutation, and elimination operators used in EMA were also applied in NNIA, NSGA-II and NSGA-III. In addition, the EMA, NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III were assigned the same key parameter values, which were as follows: POP\_size = 150, CR\_rate = 0.7, MU\_rate = 0.4, $L S \_ r a t e = 0 . 1 5 .$ . For each instance, each algorithm was run 10 times independently under the stop criterion of 100 iterations. Then we recorded the average time, while computing each benchmark with the four algorithms, and defined the minimum average time as the time stop criterion. Table 7 shows the time results of the four algorithms under the iteration stop criterion, in which the bold numbers denote the time stop criterion for each benchmark. In the second stage, we reran the EMA, NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III algorithms for each instance under the corresponding time stop criterion obtained in the first step. Finally, a comparison of the results based on the C-metric and the IGD are shown in Tables 7 and 8 respectively. The superior results are highlighted in bold. In Table 8, a comparison of the results between the NNIA and EMA can be found from columns 3–4. For all the 40 instances, the EMA obtained better solutions than the NNIA barring DFM05, DFM11, and DFM20. From columns 5–8 in Table 8, we can see the results of the EMA vs NSGA-II and EMA vs NSGA-III. The EMA acquired better performance for each benchmark compared to either of the NSGAs, since the solutions computed by the EMA always dominated the solutions obtained by the NSGA-II and NSGA-III. Consequently, a comparison of the C-metric reflects that the performance of the EMA was better than those of NSGA-II and NSGA-III in solving the DFJSPT. Table 9 reveals the IGD comparison results of the four algorithms under the time stop criterion. For small-sized instances (DFM01–15), excluding DFM5–6, DFM10–11, and DFM15, twothirds of the calculation results were equal to 0, which implies that no solution in the EMA was dominated by solutions obtained by NNIA, NSGA-II, or NSGA-III. As far as the middle instances (DFM16–30) were concerned, better results were obtained with the proposed EMA than for the small instances, and only two instances (DFM18 and DFM20) did not yield good results. In addition, the EMA stood out among the four algorithms as completely dominant results were obtained from DFM31 to DFM40. Based on the above analysis, we can conclude that the proposed EMA yielded a better performance than the NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III for solving the DFJSPT. To ensure that the comparison results were more transparent, a popular Pareto frontier (PF) chart (Kacem, Hammadi, & Borne, 2002) was drawn to present the performances of the EMA, NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III. Six random examples that included DFM01, DFM14, DFM18, DFM30, DFM 33, and DFM39, were selected from the small, medium, and large size benchmarks, and the results are depicted in Fig. 9. From Fig. 9, we observe that the EMA could obtain more uniform solutions than the other three algorithms, implying that the EMA had a better stability during the computations. Furthermore, it can be seen that the solutions from the EMA, as shown in Fig. 9(a)–(f) were closer to the bottom of the plots, implying that the EMA’s solution set had a high probability of dominating those of the NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III. Thus, the PF charts indicate that the EMA has advantages in solving the DFJSPT compared to the other algorithms, which is also in agreement with the previous results. Next, the convergence charts of the three objectives are drawn to illustrate the behavior of the four algorithms. Fig. 10 shows the convergence results of DFM14 and DFM18, which were selected randomly from the 40 comparison results. From Fig. 10 (a) and (d), it can be observed that the EMA had an excellent convergence rate and the best initial solution among all the four algorithms for objective OF1. For objective OF2 shown in Fig. 10 (b) and (e), the performance of the EMA was even better. However, according to Fig. 10 (c) and (f), the fastest convergence was obtained with the NNIA, which was superior even to that of the EMA. It indicates that
